The UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermaths of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.

The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement.

"The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement.

UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV."

UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light.

"In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find."

UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars, however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas.

Supernovas occur when a massive star runs out of fuel for nuclear fusion and can no longer support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the core of the star collapses, its outer layers are blasted outward in cosmic explosions we call supernovas.

This is a process that scientists are keen to understand, as these explosions fling the heavy elements forged during the stars' lifetimes into surrounding galaxies. This material becomes the building blocks of the next generation of stars, planets, and possibly even life.

UVEX will also investigate what happens to the end products of some supernovas, neutron stars, when they meet and merge.

Neutron stars contain between one and two times the mass of the sun crammed into a width of around 12 miles (20 kilometers). That means they are composed of matter so dense that, if a teaspoon of it were brought to Earth, it would weigh over 1 billion tons. That's equivalent to stacking around 9 million adult blue whales on a spoon.

So, when neutron stars in binary systems spiral together and merge, they create an environment so violent that it's the only place in the universe where scientists are sure that elements heavier than lead, like gold, silver, and platinum, are able to be forged.

Currently, neutron star mergers are detected via ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves. Scientists can then follow up on the aftermath of the mergers by observing them in electromagnetic light, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. Thus, UVEX will add another aspect to the investigation of neutron star collisions and our understanding of where heavy elements originate.

The new space telescope's maneuverability will allow it to observe these explosive events very shortly after they happen, giving it an advantage over other instruments, including NASA's long-serving Hubble Space Telescope.

"With UVEX, we will now be able to follow up on gravitational-wave events in ultraviolet light," UVEX team member and Caltech scientist Mansi Kasliwal said in the same statement. "I can count on two hands how many spectra we have of transient events in their infancy phase with the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble is, of course, amazing and does have some ultraviolet capabilities, but it cannot rapidly pivot to observe real-time events."

UVEX will also be revolutionary in the study of blue stars that have had their outer layers of hydrogen stripped away by companion stars. These stars offer researchers a unique opportunity to study the interior of stars, which is usually obscured by their outer layers.

"We will be able to see what's inside the stars," Kareem El-Badry, an associate professor of astronomy at Caltech and a member of the UVEX team, said in the same statement. "We only know of a small number of stripped stars of this type now. UVEX will find hundreds."

All of the above elements discussed are the expected discoveries and investigations that UVEX will be involved with. Perhaps even more exciting, however, are the unexpected elements of the universe it will uncover.

"Every time you look at the skies in a new wavelength, you learn something new and unexpected," El-Badry said.

#725. A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid

Scientists have demonstrated an extraordinary form of quantum matter that combines two properties that seem incompatible. Known as a supersolid, this unusual state has the orderly structure of a crystal while also displaying the frictionless flow associated with a special kind of liquid. Even more remarkably, researchers have now observed this behavior at room temperature, eliminating the need for the extreme cooling traditionally used to investigate such phenomena.

The breakthrough was achieved by an international team from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). Rather than relying on atoms cooled to temperatures near absolute zero, the scientists created a supersolid using particles that combine properties of light and matter.

Published in Science Advances, the findings introduce a new way to investigate exotic quantum behavior under much more accessible conditions. They could also help advance future technologies ranging from optical computing to highly sensitive sensors.

How Can Matter Behave Like Both a Solid and a Liquid?

Under ordinary circumstances, solids and liquids behave very differently. Crystals have an organized internal structure, with their particles arranged in repeating patterns. Liquids, by comparison, can flow and change shape.

Quantum physics, however, allows matter to behave in ways that would be impossible under the familiar rules of everyday life.

One example is superfluidity, a remarkable phenomenon in which a fluid loses its viscosity, or internal resistance to flowing. A superfluid can move through extremely narrow passages without experiencing the usual friction. Imagine placing an oar into such a liquid. You would encounter almost no resistance until the oar reached a certain speed. Beyond that threshold, tiny swirling structures known as quantum vortices would suddenly form.

During the 1960s, physicists proposed an even stranger possibility. What if a superfluid could also develop the repeating internal structure normally associated with a crystal?

This hypothetical combination became known as a supersolid. In such a state, the material exhibits the spatial organization of a solid while retaining the remarkable flow properties of a superfluid.

For decades, supersolidity remained a theoretical concept. Experimental confirmation finally arrived in 2017, when researchers observed the phenomenon in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. These condensates form when particles enter a collective quantum state and begin behaving as a coordinated system rather than as separate individuals.

The catch was that producing these conditions generally required sophisticated equipment capable of cooling matter to temperatures extremely close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

Creating a Quantum Supersolid Using Light Instead of Cold Atoms

The international TopoLight consortium approached the challenge from a different direction. Instead of using ultracold atoms, the researchers worked with unusual hybrid particles called exciton polaritons.

These quasiparticles arise when light interacts so strongly with matter that the two become coupled inside a tiny optical chamber called a microcavity. The resulting particles display characteristics of both light and matter.

Exciton polaritons are extremely short-lived, typically surviving for only a few picoseconds. A picosecond is one trillionth of a second. Despite their brief existence, these particles can organize into a Bose-Einstein condensate and collectively exhibit the behavior of a quantum superfluid.

To create the necessary conditions, the team constructed an optical microcavity containing a specially engineered liquid crystal and covered it with an organic semiconductor. The arrangement allowed light and matter to interact strongly enough to produce the desired quantum effects without the need for extreme cooling.

"Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C," says Professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures.

That temperature is approximately 140°F, far above the freezing conditions normally associated with experiments involving exotic quantum matter.

Strange Patterns of Light Reveal a Supersolid

How can researchers determine whether a collection of particles has entered such an unusual state?

In this experiment, the evidence appeared in the light emitted by the sample. When the system transitioned into the supersolid phase, researchers observed a series of regularly spaced bright fringes.

These patterns indicated that the particle condensate had spontaneously developed a repeating variation in its density. This type of spatial organization is a defining feature of crystalline structures and an important sign of supersolidity.

But the researchers noticed another intriguing effect.

Each time a laser pulse excited the sample, the bright fringes appeared in a different position. Rather than following a single fixed arrangement, the quantum system repeatedly selected among several equally possible configurations.

"This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking," explains Professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). "Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed."

Spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs when a system that could exist in several equivalent arrangements settles into one particular configuration. In this case, the effect became visible through the changing positions of the light patterns.

The condensate also displayed another unusual characteristic called a persistent spin helix. This refers to a repeating variation in the polarization of the emitted light. Polarization describes the orientation of light's oscillating electric field.

Together, these observations revealed two different forms of order occurring at the same time. One appeared in the intensity of the emitted light, while the other appeared in its polarization.

A Difficult Experiment With Only Hours to Succeed

Achieving these results required overcoming an unexpected practical obstacle.

The organic semiconductor used in the device gradually reacted with the liquid crystal. As a result, the experimental samples had a limited useful lifetime, giving the scientists only a few hours to collect their measurements after assembly.

This restriction made careful preparation essential. The researchers needed to determine exactly which measurements to perform and in what order before beginning each experimental run.

"We had to plan the entire sequence of experiments in advance," recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper's first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. "Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample."

The most important measurements took place at IBM Research Zurich. There, scientists deposited thin layers of the organic semiconductor onto specialized structures designed to manipulate light. These photonic structures had been manufactured at the Military University of Technology.

The semiconductor itself was not new to the researchers. IBM scientists had investigated its quantum properties for years, including its ability to support Bose-Einstein condensation.

"We have studied the organic semiconductor MeLPPP (methyl-substituted ladder-type poly(paraphenylene) for many years and previously observed Bose-Einstein condensation in this material," says Thilo Stöferle from IBM Research. "This was the first time we combined it with a liquid-crystal microcavity."

Bringing these materials together ultimately made it possible to observe the unusual supersolid behavior at room temperature.

Why Room Temperature Quantum Matter Matters

The significance of the discovery extends beyond demonstrating another unusual phenomenon predicted by quantum physics.

Many experiments involving exotic quantum states depend on costly cryogenic systems designed to maintain temperatures close to absolute zero. These demanding conditions make research more complicated and can create substantial obstacles when scientists attempt to turn laboratory discoveries into useful technologies.

The new results show that certain exotic quantum effects can instead be investigated in photonic devices that operate at ordinary temperatures.

This could create opportunities for future technologies that use light to process information. Potential applications include ultrafast photonic devices, specialized computing accelerators inspired by the way biological brains process information, and advanced optical sensors.

The computing approach, known as neuromorphic computing, seeks to imitate aspects of the brain's information processing to perform certain tasks more efficiently. Light-based systems could eventually provide new ways to accelerate these operations.

The supersolid's exceptional sensitivity to light polarization may also prove useful for developing sensors capable of detecting extremely subtle optical changes.

These applications remain possibilities for future research, but the ability to generate the underlying quantum behavior without extreme cooling represents an important step toward making such technologies more practical.

Electrically Controlled Quantum Matter Opens New Possibilities

One of the most promising features of the experiment is that the optical device can be adjusted using electricity.

The liquid crystal microcavities provide the first electrically tunable platform for studying supersolid exciton-polariton condensates. This means researchers can alter the optical properties of the system by applying an external voltage.

Earlier experimental approaches did not offer this same degree of electrical control.

The ability to adjust the system dynamically gives physicists greater flexibility when investigating how quantum states emerge, interact, and respond to changing conditions.

It could also become valuable when designing practical quantum photonic devices, where precise control over the behavior of light and matter is essential.

By combining room-temperature operation with electrical tunability, the researchers have established a versatile platform for exploring quantum phenomena that previously required far more demanding experimental conditions.

About the University of Warsaw Faculty of Physics

The University of Warsaw has a long history of research and education in physics and astronomy. Both disciplines became part of the university in 1816, when they were included in the Faculty of Philosophy. The university subsequently established its Astronomical Observatory in 1825.

Today, the Faculty of Physics includes the Institutes of Experimental Physics, Theoretical Physics, and Geophysics, along with the Department of Mathematical Methods in Physics.

Its research encompasses nearly every major area of modern physics, from the behavior of particles at quantum scales to the structure and evolution of the universe.

The faculty employs more than 250 academic teachers and serves approximately 1,350 students and more than 150 doctoral students.

According to Shanghai's Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, the University of Warsaw ranks among the world's top 150 institutions for physics education.

Materials provided by University of Warsaw, Faculty of Physics. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#724. Gwen Stefani & Gavin Rossdale Reunite to Support Son Kingston at His L.A. Concert Alongside Blake Shelton

The exes split in 2015, and the No Doubt frontwoman married her Voice co-star six years later.

After all that they’ve been through, Gwen Stefani and Gavin Rossdale are cool — at least, cool enough to reunite to support their son Kingston at his recent concert, with the No Doubt frontwoman attending with husband Blake Shelton at her side.

The three musicians were all in the audience Tuesday night at The Troubadour in West Hollywood, California, as Stefani and Rossdale’s eldest son rocked out onstage, according to photos circulating online. TMZ also shared video of Shelton and his fellow The Voice coaching alum holding hands as they left the venue, with Stefani at one point saying goodbye to her parents before getting into her car.

Rossdale was also captured interacting with fans and signing autographs outside of the venue, at one point telling paparazzi that while he might love to perform with Kingston someday, his son “doesn’t want anything to do with me musically.”

“He wants to do his own [thing],” the Bush rocker said proudly. “He’s really big on that. I was lucky I was even allowed to come.”

Stefani and Rossdale also share younger sons Zuma and Apollo. They got married after six years of dating in 2002 before filing for divorce in 2015.

“I never thought I’d ever get divorced,” Rossdale said on the Amy and T.J. podcast in 2024. “Sometimes I wish that, when you see the kids, there’s a loss. It would be nice if there was more of a connection with the person that made them with me.”

The “Just a Girl” singer would go on to marry Shelton in 2021 after they met on The Voice. The pair recently returned to the singing competition series for its 30th-anniversary special, which aired in September.

Kingston is clearly paving his own way in music, taking after his famous parents. The 20-year-old’s show at The Troubadour came a few days after the release of his EP Louise Street.

“Last night was amazing!!” he wrote on his Instagram Story the day after his concert. “Huge thank you to everyone that showed up love you guys can’t wait for the next one.”

#722. Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years

Scientists have discovered remarkably preserved traces of dinosaur blood inside 115-million-year-old bones, revealing that delicate biological molecules can survive far longer than previously believed. The breakthrough could transform how researchers study prehistoric animals and even influence the search for ancient life beyond Earth.

An international team led by Curtin University found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules in the remains of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod dinosaur discovered in northeastern Brazil. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also include amino acids associated with collagen, an important structural protein found in bones and other connective tissues.

The discovery provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of molecules derived from hemoglobin inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. Earlier research had identified structures resembling blood cells in ancient fossils, but scientists had not conclusively demonstrated the presence of these particular molecular remains within them.

Ancient Dinosaur Blood Preserved Inside Fossilized Bones

When researchers examined the dinosaur's limb bones, they identified numerous mineralized red blood cells inside vascular canals, the tiny passages that once contained blood vessels. Chemical analysis revealed preserved heme molecules, which are components of hemoglobin, the protein that allows red blood cells to transport oxygen.

Finding these molecules provided direct chemical evidence that the fossil contained remnants of ancient blood. It also demonstrated that some biological materials once thought too fragile to survive for millions of years can remain detectable under exceptional conditions.

The study was led by John Curtin Distinguished Professor Kliti Grice, founding director of Curtin University's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre and an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellow.

"To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: this really is a landmark discovery," Professor Grice said.

"It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in."

How Dinosaur Blood Survived 115 Million Years

The extraordinary preservation appears to be connected to a mineral called hausmannite. This mineral helped stabilize the fossilized blood cells and preserve their molecular components (including amino acids of collagen) over an immense span of geological time.

In effect, the mineral created a natural time capsule that protected microscopic evidence of the dinosaur's biology long after its death.

Researchers believe the conditions surrounding the dinosaur's burial were also crucial. They suspect the animal was quickly covered by sediment in an environment with little oxygen and abundant microbial activity. These conditions may have helped preserve biological material that would ordinarily have broken down and disappeared.

The international research effort brought together scientists from Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University.

A Discovery That Challenges Fossil Preservation Limits

The findings challenge a longstanding assumption in paleontology that molecules associated with blood, particularly those derived from hemoglobin, could not remain preserved across such enormous periods of time.

Beyond confirming the survival of ancient blood components, the discovery raises the possibility that other fossils may contain molecular information that conventional examinations have overlooked.

"These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time," Professor Grice said.

"It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level paleontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals."

Such information could eventually help researchers better understand how extinct animals functioned, including aspects of their metabolism and physiology that are difficult to reconstruct from bones alone.

Implications for Ancient Life Beyond Earth

The significance of the discovery may extend well beyond dinosaurs. Understanding how fragile biological structures can survive for millions of years could also help scientists identify possible traces of ancient life in other extreme environments, including those beyond Earth.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, said the results are changing how researchers understand the preservation of molecular structures over vast timescales and under harsh conditions.

These insights could be valuable to astrobiology, a field that investigates the possibility of life elsewhere in the universe. If biological molecules or their chemical signatures can persist under the right conditions for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to reconsider where and how they look for evidence of ancient organisms.

"This study exemplifies how coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines can unlock extraordinary insights into ancient life," Professor Van Kranendonk said.

The research was supported by a 2021 Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Professor Grice.

The study, titled "Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115- million-year-old dinosaur bone," was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

This dazzling collection of ancient stars could hold clues to the Milky Way's past.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange.

But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed.

The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus.

M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity.

Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old!

Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell.

Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history.

Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

ILLIT scores its first No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Album Sales chart as the act’s new EP BREAK EVEN starts atop the list dated Nov. 14. The four-song project sold 32,000 copies in the United States in the week ending Nov. 5, according to Luminate, marking the group’s largest sales week to date.

In total, BREAK EVEN is ILLIT’s fifth top 10, all achieved consecutively, on the Top Album Sales chart.

BREAK EVEN’s album sales were largely driven by its availability across more than 24 CD variants (all containing collectible items such as photocards, stickers and posters, with some randomized).

Elsewhere in a very busy top 10 on the latest Top Album Sales chart, Queens of the Stone Age’s Perfecth starts at No. 2, landing the rock band it sixth top 10. Michael Jackson’s Thriller surges 14-3 following the classic set’s reissue on three vinyl variants and cassette tape. Nickelback captures its ninth top 10 with the arrival of Everything Under the Sun at No. 5.

IVE notches its first top 10 on Top Album Sales, and best sales week, as Looks Can Kill enters at No. 6 with 10,000 sold. Rock band blink-182 sees its 2001 album Take Off Your Pants and Jacket reenters at No. 8 after it was reissued on vinyl for its 25th anniversary. Another album that got a 25th anniversary reissue, Mariah Carey’s Glitter soundtrack, also reenters at No. 9.

Rounding out the top 10 is $uicideboy$’ 2020 album Stop Staring at the Shadows, which debuts at No. 10 following its first vinyl release.

Billboard’s Top Album Sales chart ranks the top-selling albums of the week based only on pure album sales (physical and digital download purchases combined). The chart’s history dates to May 25, 1991, the first week Billboard began tabulating charts with electronically monitored piece count information from SoundScan, now Luminate. Pure album sales were the sole measurement utilized by the Billboard 200 albums chart through the list dated Dec. 6, 2014, after which that chart switched to a methodology that blends album sales with track equivalent album (TEA) units and streaming equivalent album (SEA) units.

#719. Amanda Seyfried Feared ‘You Can See Everything’ Could “Destroy” Her Career, Says Her Opinion of Billy Evans “Only Got Worse”

The actress is finally — really — opening up about her involvement in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's documentary. "There was no reason for him to get that aggressive," she said of Elizabeth Holmes' partner.

[This story contains spoilers from You Can See Everything.]

Amanda Seyfried is finally — really — opening up about her involvement in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, You Can See Everything, including why she feared the project could negatively impact her career and her tense confrontation with Elizabeth Holmes‘ husband, Billy Evans.

Following the A24 film’s release nearly a month ago, Seyfried has largely avoided directly addressing her surprise appearance in You Can See Everything. In the film’s third act, she reprises her portrayal of Holmes, the disgraced Theranos founder, whom she played in the limited series The Dropout — a role that earned her an Emmy in 2022. Related Stories SCAD Savannah Film Festival "It's All Cinema!" Directors of 2026's Top Docs on Taking Risks, Interacting With Subjects and the Huge Success of 'You Can See Everything' (Video) Movies 'You Can See Everything' Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards

In a new interview with Rolling Stone published Wednesday, Seyfried, Fielder and Oppenheim discuss the film’s full spoilers for the first time, including how the actress became involved in the project and her experience meeting Evans.

While filming the documentary, which chronicles Holmes’ life in the month leading up to her prison sentence, Fielder and Oppenheim began considering how to continue the film. That’s when they came up with the idea to bring Seyfried into the project. Fielder got the actress’ phone number through his The Curse co-star Emma Stone, and the pair eventually connected over Zoom, where he showed her footage from the film.

“I remember when [Emma] texted, and I was like, ‘Nathan Fielder? Ooh, I wonder if he wants to make something with me?’ My sister is a big fan [of yours, Nathan], and I know a lot of people are big fans of Nathan for You. I’d only seen The Curse. When you said you had 90 minutes of footage for me to see and help you work through, I was like, ‘Oh, he just wants some advice. He just wants us to know about my experience playing her and researching her and going into the mind of that quote-unquote character I portrayed,'” the actress recalled. “After the Zoom, I was totally game to do whatever you needed. It was just your energy [that persuaded me], and how much time you had spent [on this project], and that nobody knew this was happening.”

Seyfried said she wasn’t initially nervous about joining the project because she already had a “strange level of trust” with Fielder and Oppenheim. However, she acknowledged that agreeing to participate without first consulting her representatives wasn’t the typical process.

“I would say there was a lot of risk in the back of my head, and then when I told my agent and lawyer that I had already done it? Not the normal process,” she said. “But I go off and do my own thing sometimes, and nobody had any say or control over what I was doing with Nathan and Lance. My lawyer was like, ‘Well, now we have to retroactively set your deal in place because you need protection.’ We weren’t even considering reenactments at that point.”

Seyfried ultimately reprised her portrayal of Holmes through “muscle memory,” but the actress also worried about the potential professional consequences of participating in the documentary. Fielder emphasized that she had no creative control over the project or the footage that was filmed.

“No approval. Whatsoever,” she said. “There was always this vibration of risk and that sensation of: Am I going to destroy my career in some way? Am I going to get entangled in this, like, wasp’s nest with Billy? Am I gonna say the wrong thing? Am I gonna perpetuate negativity for her? Everything was scary.”

Seyfried also explained why she wanted to meet Evans after watching footage of his interactions with Holmes and the filmmakers.

“It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings. What he was doing and how he was in the footage that I saw, how you guys were interacting — it felt yucky to me,” she said. “I just wanted any information I could get on Billy. I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy. It was exciting to me, and it was scary, and it was questionable.”

Her opinion of Evans, however, “only got worse” after they met. “I do not like him,” she said.

The actress also met Holmes and Evans’ children during the documentary, in a scene that was interrupted by a phone call from Holmes herself, who was calling from prison. Seyfried recalled that the filmmakers weren’t expecting the call to come at that moment, adding that it really was Holmes on the other end.

Oppenheim also pointed to the tense dinner scene between Seyfried, Fielder and Evans, during which Evans criticizes the actress’ performance and they get into an argument over Seyfried’s criticisms of the late Charlie Kirk.

“The moment that I’ll probably be thinking about on my deathbed is the dinner scene between you and Billy,” Oppenheim said.

“There was no reason for him to get that aggressive,” Seyfried said. “That’s the word I’m going to use, as it’s more diplomatic. If my jaw wasn’t obviously on the floor, you could tell, like, it had come unhinged. I don’t want to provoke him, but at this point, it’s kind of like, the gloves are off. Because this guy has disrespected me in such a way that I was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think so, buddy.'”

She continued, “I don’t like the way he’s using this human being, his wife — the person he says he’s ‘building monuments of love’ to — as a tool. Maybe he does respect her, but he’s behaving like he does not respect her. And not only am I protective of myself, I’m just trying to set the record straight in a way where I’m trying to defend myself, too, while maintaining some kind of rapport with him, so I can stay and he doesn’t kick us out, you know?”

Despite her concerns about the project, Seyfried said she has no regrets about participating: “I don’t regret it at all. I’m having the time of my life right now!”

#718. NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary era of astronomical discovery to a close. The spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a mission that lasted more than ten times longer than originally planned.

Launched in 2004, Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes designed to study some of the most powerful explosions in the universe. Its instruments could detect different types of light, allowing scientists to investigate energetic cosmic events that would be difficult to understand using a single telescope.

NASA's Swift Observatory Re-Enters Earth's Atmosphere

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.

NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere. However, officials acknowledged that some components might have survived the intense heat of re-entry.

A Two-Year NASA Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years

Swift was originally developed to investigate gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily powerful flashes of high-energy radiation associated with some of the most extreme events in the cosmos. These bursts can occur when massive stars collapse or when certain compact objects, such as neutron stars, merge.

Although NASA initially planned for Swift to operate for just two years, the observatory continued making scientific contributions for more than two decades.

One of its most important capabilities was its ability to respond quickly to sudden cosmic events. When Swift detected an energetic outburst, it could rapidly redirect its telescopes toward the source and notify observatories around the world. This coordinated approach allowed astronomers to study brief astronomical phenomena before they faded from view.

Swift also observed multiple wavelengths of light, giving researchers different ways to examine the same event and better understand the physical processes behind it.

Over its remarkably long lifetime, Swift's scientific contributions expanded far beyond its original focus on gamma-ray bursts.

The observatory helped astronomers investigate active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars that produce powerful X-ray flares, and supernovae, the enormous explosions that mark the deaths of certain stars.

Its observations also extended much closer to home, including studies of comets and asteroids within our own solar system.

By combining rapid observations with the ability to detect different forms of radiation, Swift became a valuable tool for exploring both distant cosmic explosions and nearby objects. Its re-entry marks the end of a mission that greatly exceeded its planned lifespan and helped transform scientists' understanding of some of the universe's most energetic phenomena.

#717. Summer Walker Countersued by LVRN for Commissions and Royalties: ‘Stubbornly Litigious’

The label/management firm says Walker has breached their contract. Her lawyer told Billboard the new claims are "disappointing."

Summer Walker’s longtime label/management firm LVRN is countersuing the singer over unpaid commissions and royalties.

The R&B singer sued LVRN in August, accusing the Atlanta-based indie music company of skimming money from her music, touring and merch. LVRN denies those claims and, in a new court filing, says Walker is actually the one who breached their 2017 contract by refusing to share key cuts of her earnings.

“Walker has acted in bad faith and been stubbornly litigious,” write LVRN’s lawyers in a Monday (Nov. 9) countersuit, obtained by Billboard.

LVRN alleges that Walker hasn’t delivered on several percentage cuts set forth in her contract, including a 7% commission from her Still Finally Over It arena tour this year, a 20% share of her public performance royalties and a 15% management commission on gross ancillary income.

The legal documents do not specify which business deals are missing that 15% commission to LVRN. But they list more than two dozen “lucrative” opportunities LVRN negotiated for Walker — including a partnership with Rihanna’s Savage x Fenty brand, her opening act slot on Chris Brown’s Breezy Bowl stadium tour and a performance at the FIFA World Cup this year.

LVRN is now seeking unspecified financial damages from Walker for breach of contract. The singer’s attorney, Keith Moten, tells Billboard on Wednesday (Nov. 11) that the counterclaim “does nothing to change the fundamental issues at the heart of Summer’s lawsuit, nor does it diminish their obligation to account for their actions.”

“It is particularly disappointing that, rather than meaningfully addressing Summer’s serious allegations, LVRN is now seeking additional money from the very artist whose talent, hard work and success helped build its business,” adds Moten. “We strongly dispute LVRN’s counterclaims and remain confident in the legal and factual grounds supporting Summer’s lawsuit. She remains steadfast in her pursuit of accountability, fairness and the freedom to move forward with her career on her terms. We intend to vigorously pursue those objectives through the courts.”

Walker has been pursuing legal claims since this summer in the hopes of severing her contracts with both LVRN and Interscope Records, to whom she jointly signed in 2017. Separately from the LVRN lawsuit, Walker sent a notice to the Universal Music Group subsidiary in August invoking her rights under California’s seven-year statute, a state law that allows individuals to cut off any personal contract that runs past that amount of time.

But the law has a catch: labels can sue for damages if an artist chooses to exit a record deal after seven years but before all of their album commitments have been fulfilled. Interscope did just that last month, filing a $50 million lawsuit alleging Walker has only delivered three projects from her contract’s five-album commitment: her 2019 debut Over It, which hit No. 2 on the Billboard 200, the 2021 chart-topper Still Over It and another No. 2 set, Finally Over It, in 2025.

Interscope has said it’s “hopeful that our ongoing discussions will lead to an amicable resolution” with Walker. Moten, who’s also representing Walker in the Interscope case, previously told Billboard he was preparing to countersue the major label but still “remains open to a constructive resolution.”

#716. After ‘DWTS’ Season 35, Mark Ballas Would Love His Wife BC Jean to Be His Next Celebrity Partner

The veteran ‘DWTS’ pro speaks with THR about how he juggles his music and dance career, taking on season 35 with his ‘Traitors’ co-star Maura Higgins and hopes of potentially doing the show with wife.

Mark Ballas likes to take things day by day.

The Dancing With the Stars professional dancer appeared on seasons five through 22 consecutively, popped back in for season 25, then took a break before appearing on season 31 with Charli D’Amelio. Ballas then returned for last year’s 34th season to compete with Whitney Leavitt, and is back on the pro dancer cast for season 35.

There’s no method to how he decides when the timing is right for him to appear on DWTS. “It’s all about timing, and obviously if the show wants to have me, and where I’m at creatively,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter. Related Stories TV Trisha Paytas to Host Queer Dating Show 'Don't Date Alone,' Debuting in Early 2027 (Exclusive) TV 'Grey's Anatomy' Texas Spinoff Casts Karla Souza in Lead Role

Last year, his partnership with the former Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star was so shiny it led to their box-office breaking stint on Broadway in Chicago together. Since season 34, Ballas hasn’t had a moment to slow down, going on to judge the DWTS spinoff The Next Pro.

He also made an appearance on Emmy juggernaut The Traitors, where he met his season 35 celebrity partner Maura Higgins. When asked about what his future with DWTS could look like, Ballas doesn’t have many concrete answers: Would he join a potential second season of The Next Pro? “If the timing feels right and everything’s in line with my family, and it makes sense, then sure,” Ballas responds.

Would he join the main DWTS judging panel in the future? “I’d have to see,” he says. “I’m a very take it day-by-day person.”

One question he has a sure answer for is what celebrity he’d potentially want to do another season of DWTS with: His wife, singer-songwriter BC Jean. “That would be a riot,” he says.

Below, Ballas opens up about the growth of DWTS over the years; his partnership with Leavitt that expanded all the way to Broadway (and if she’s asked him to film for her new Hulu reality show); season 35 with Higgins; and how he balances his career as a musician and dancer.

You were a judge on the first season of The Next Pro. Because of that, I wondered if you would want to return as a pro after moving into that judging slot. You’ve judged before, but what specifically made you want to come back as a pro for season 35?

I don’t know if there’s anything specific. They are two different shows. Next Pro is about finding a new pro and judging based on if the contestants have all the bits and bobs, as you would say, to be a pro on the show, because it’s more than being a dancer. There’s lots of nuance to being a pro. So I don’t look at them as the same. I’ve only guest judged once. I love the creative part of the show. That’s what makes it fun. That’s kind of been my life for so long. And one of the big reasons for me going back last season was excitement for my son to see me do what I’ve dedicated my life to. He’s only three, but he can watch the show and he’s like, “Oh my God, dada!” So it’s a big part of it, and constantly loving the new challenges and creativity. It’s pretty straightforward, simple as that, really.

There’s been speculation about whether The Next Pro would come back and do another season. If they do a second season and asked you to come back as a judge, is that something that you would be interested in?

I don’t know if they’re doing a second season yet. I’ve had no confirmation of that. But yeah, again, if the timing feels right and everything’s in line with my family, and it makes sense, then sure. It was a fun experience.

Last season, your partnership with Whitney sparked such a huge conversation while you were competing on the show. What was it like going from that season where your partnership sparked so much conversation, so much so that it laid the foundation for you to extend your professional relationship all the way to Broadway for Chicago?

Yeah, I think that whole thing was just very serendipitous. It kind of just organically happened. When we did the Chicago number on [DWTS], you had to pick a song that had been previously used on the show. We got a list, and you had to grab one from there. We were at the time in the competition where Argentine tango felt right. So then when “Cell Block Tango” popped up, it was like, “That’s a great option.” And then Whitney already had auditions lined up for Chicago, and I had been talking to Chicago in the past, because I’ve done other Broadway shows too. I did Jersey Boys and Kinky Boots. I did my theater training in England, and that was kind of where I started in the industry. I did some other musicals in the U.K. It’s another big part of my life, and Chicago is one of my all-time favorite shows, so it all honestly was so organic.

We did that number, and she did so well. She had her audition. Obviously, her audition went really well. She booked that role, and then I got called in for an audition too. It went well as well, and it just so happened the timing worked out. There was a time where potentially we weren’t going to do [Chicago] together because of Next Pro, but it ended up working out. We had such a laugh doing the show, and Chicago is kind of Broadway royalty of a show, so it was a huge honor.

It was just announced that Whitney is getting her own reality show. Has she asked you to film anything for it? And if not, if she did ask, would you do that?

I’m not going to spill her business. (Laughs.)

You and Maura were on The Traitors ahead of Dancing With the Stars season 35. What has the experience been like taking on two massive shows back to back together?

It’s been fun. Me and Maura had a great time in the castle. That whole experience was so great. Traitors is unlike anything I’ve ever done. Imagine going over to your friend’s house and playing Mafia, and it doesn’t end for three weeks. (Laughs.) I remember in the castle, Maura being like, “I would love to do Dancing With the Stars one day.” Again, another one of those things: If you’d asked me at the time when we were shooting Traitors if I would be on a season of Dancing with one of my castmates, I probably wouldn’t have believed you. Again, another one of those unexpected, cool things that happen.

Grammy Night is particularly special because you are a musician yourself. At this point in your career, how do you balance both the music and dance sides of your career?

Well, it’s funny you ask that, because my wife and I are in the middle of creating a new record, an album. We’ve been working on it since our son was born, so it’s been a work in progress. We’ve gotten, I’d say, half of it done, which is pretty cool, but it is hard to do both. When we’re in season, all the focus goes into [DWTS]. But we’re close to the end now, and once this is done, [we’ll] probably take a little bit of a break and reopen the record and see where it’s at, see if we’re still feeling it, and make any changes we need to, and get ready to release songs pretty soon. We got some really good ones that we’re very excited about, but we’ve written so many. We’re constantly changing our board, or our track listing. Some go on, some go off.

Your wife has made a few appearances in the ballroom this year, singing live vocals for you and Maura. What has it been like having her in the ballroom?

It’s been great. She sang on the show a couple times in the past, which has been cool. When she came on to sing “Black Velvet,” that was kind of a happy accident, because our original singer, Travis Garland, made it pretty far on America’s Got Talent, and the show overlaps. So last minute, BC [Jean] stepped in to save the day. It’s kind of a cool out-of-body experience to be hearing her voice as I’m performing, and there’s a sense of love and home and comfort there. We had her sing on the Lost Boys song as well for Halloween Night, which is really good. She’s my favorite-sounding voice ever. It’s a really, really, really cool moment.

Looking at the growth and spike in popularity that Dancing With the Stars has experienced over the past few years, you are somebody who has been around from the very early seasons; is there anything you can pinpoint that has been the biggest change in the show over the years?

It’s kind of like anything, really. It just evolves. The production, the way it moves, the content of it all is just bigger. It’s really, really grown, and it’s pretty cool to see new people getting into the show for the first time. It’s pretty wild. But the heartbeat of the show is the same. It’s still about ballroom dancing, and predominantly the 10 ballroom dances, which are waltz, tango, foxtrot, quickstep, Viennese waltz, cha-cha, samba, rumba, paso and jive, and then there’s a couple of speciality dances in there. At the end of the day, what started the whole thing is, it’s a ballroom show. Ballroom dancing is such a niche thing, but it brings so many people together. And if you’re fortunate enough to go deep into the show, it’s something that you’ll take with you forever.

Who do you think would be more likely to become a Dancing With the Stars permanent judge first, you or your mother, Shirley Ballas?

I have no idea. She’s already a judge on Strictly. That would be difficult to do both, but Len [Goodman] did it for so long. So did Bruno [Tonioli]. I have no idea what the intentions are with the panel. I think the panel is pretty set.

In the future, would you be open to potentially becoming a permanent Dancing With the Stars judge one day?

I don’t know. I’m not sure. I’d have to see. I’m a very take it day-by-day person. Honestly, I don’t think ahead like that. I’d have to see if it came along. I enjoyed guest judging. The Next Pro was really fun. I think I’ve done the show for long enough that I could give good feedback and advice for contestants. But, again, that’s totally out of my hands.

What is your favorite part of a full week in Dancing With the Stars: the choreography, teaching/rehearsing, dress rehearsal or the live show day?

Probably that feeling when you’ve got the routine down to music. Because the teaching part and the choreography, it’s a lot of trial and error, and it takes time, it takes nuance. But that feeling when you get your partner through it the first time to music and seeing how excited they are, if it goes well, that’s a pretty cool feeling as a coach. The live show was super fun, but there’s nothing like that first initial reaction, like, “I did it,” you know what I mean?

Do you have a favorite number that you’ve ever choreographed for the show?

I mean, Charli [D’Amelio]’s Viennese waltz was a really special one. There was a lot going on that week, and it was also, I think, one of the last dances I got to do for Len, too. And it was very traditional, which was what he loved.

At this point, do you have a dream celebrity dance partner that you would like to potentially do the show with?

(Laughs.) I don’t know; my wife and I always joke, I’d love to do it with her. That’d be so fun. I mean, I don’t know. Maybe the record blows up enough at some point. We could do that together. That would be a riot. That would be that fun.

#715. Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky

November 2026 is packed with celestial events worth watching, from brilliant meteors streaking across the sky to a striking encounter between Mars and Jupiter. NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is also approaching an extraordinary milestone, while a dazzling supermoon will close out the month.

Three meteor showers offer multiple opportunities to catch shooting stars, including occasional fireballs bright enough to stand out dramatically against the night sky. Meanwhile, two of the solar system's most recognizable planets will appear unusually close together just before sunrise.

As if that weren't enough, humanity's most distant spacecraft is reaching a point where radio signals from Earth take an entire day to arrive.

Here's what NASA recommends watching for in November.

Three Meteor Showers Could Light Up November's Sky

November gives skywatchers several chances to see meteors flash across the darkness. The first opportunities come from the Southern and Northern Taurids, two related meteor showers that reach their highest activity levels about a week apart.

The Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Both showers get their names from the constellation Taurus, where their meteors appear to originate when viewed from Earth.

Neither shower is especially prolific. Even under excellent conditions, each typically produces only about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally producing impressive fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors that can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.

The Leonids provide another opportunity later in the month. Their best viewing periods are expected during the early morning hours of November 17 and 18, particularly after the Moon has disappeared below the horizon. Under ideal conditions, observers could see approximately 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.

For the best chance of spotting meteors, travel somewhere away from bright city lights. Allow your eyes roughly 30 minutes to become accustomed to the darkness, then watch a broad section of the sky rather than concentrating on one small area.

Mars and Jupiter Appear Almost Side by Side

Meteor showers aren't the only reason to get outside before dawn. On November 15 and 16, Mars and Jupiter will create an eye-catching pairing in the southeastern sky.

The two planets will appear separated by only about 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the apparent width of two full Moons placed next to each other.

Jupiter will be the brighter of the two, making it relatively easy to identify. Nearby, Mars will stand out with its characteristic reddish appearance.

No telescope or binoculars will be necessary to enjoy the sight. Both planets should be readily visible to the unaided eye under suitable viewing conditions.

Although they will appear remarkably close from Earth's perspective, Mars and Jupiter remain separated by enormous distances in space. Their apparent proximity is simply a result of their positions along our line of sight.

Watching the planets over several consecutive mornings will reveal another interesting feature of their motion. They will gradually appear to move closer together before their positions shift and they begin separating again.

Voyager 1 Reaches an Extraordinary Deep Space Milestone

While November offers plenty to observe in Earth's skies, something equally remarkable is happening far beyond the planets.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is reaching a historic distance of one light-day from Earth, becoming the first human-made object ever to travel that far from our planet.

A light-day is the distance light travels through space in 24 hours. Because radio signals move at the speed of light, a message transmitted from Earth will require an entire day to reach Voyager 1 at that distance.

If the spacecraft sends a response immediately, the return signal will take another 24 hours to arrive. That means even the fastest possible round-trip communication will require approximately 48 hours.

The milestone illustrates just how far Voyager 1 has traveled since leaving Earth and how challenging it has become to communicate with a spacecraft exploring such distant regions of space.

To get a sense of the spacecraft's current direction, look toward the constellation Ophiuchus, also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling through space in that general direction, far beyond anything visible to the unaided eye.

NASA is marking the achievement on November 17 with its Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day activation, inviting people to celebrate this extraordinary accomplishment in space exploration.

November's Supermoon Begins a Three-Month Celestial Show

The final major skywatching highlight arrives on November 24, when a full supermoon will rise into the evening sky.

A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with a period when the Moon is relatively close to Earth in its orbit. Because the Moon follows a slightly elliptical path rather than a perfect circle, its distance from our planet changes throughout the month.

When a full Moon occurs near the closer portion of that orbit, it can appear somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon. Although the difference is real, it is often subtle enough that casual observers may not immediately notice it.

November's event is particularly noteworthy because it begins a sequence of three consecutive supermoons. Another will follow in December, with a third arriving in January.

For an especially memorable view, NASA recommends looking toward the eastern horizon around sunset on November 24, when the full Moon will be rising.

The Moon may seem unusually enormous when it first appears near the horizon. However, much of that dramatic impression comes from a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.

This optical effect makes the Moon appear larger when it is close to the horizon than when it is high overhead, even though its actual apparent size changes very little. The illusion can occur during any full Moon, not just a supermoon.

With three meteor showers, a close planetary pairing, a historic Voyager 1 milestone, and the beginning of a supermoon series, November offers plenty of reasons to look up and explore the night sky.

The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground.

Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027.

"Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher."

Rocket Lab is best known for Electron, a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO).

Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO.

Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control).

Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30.

The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s.

"The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said.

That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket. For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO.

The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful.

But SpaceX is phasing out the Falcon 9 — and its heavy-lift cousin, the Falcon Heavy — nonetheless, shifting all launch work over to its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which can haul more than 100 tons to LEO.

There's a real worry among folks in the space community that this massive payload capacity won't be available to them for a while. SpaceX has made it pretty clear that early Starship operations will be geared toward internal priorities — specifically, the buildout of SpaceX's Starlink V3 broadband network and its Starmind AI data-center constellation.

These will be very big jobs, even for the most powerful rocket ever built. For example, the Starlink V3 megaconstellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk. Starship can carry about 60 of these spacecraft to LEO per launch, so just building out the constellation will require about 1,700 liftoffs.

The numbers for Starmind will be even more mind-boggling, for SpaceX wants that constellation to eventually harbor a million satellites.

The coming launch bottleneck should increase demand for Electron as well as Neutron, Beck said during Monday's call. After all, many small-satellite operators have launched with SpaceX over the years, booking spots on Falcon 9 "rideshare" flights. And those opportunities are now drying up.

"The next logical alternative is of course an Electron, so we see tremendous traction there," Beck said.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #713. Netflix Poised to Buy Radford Studio Lot at Auction for Steep Discount

The purchase will reshape the entertainment giant's production and office operations in Los Angeles.

Nine months after lenders repossessed the historic Radford Studio Center lot from Hackman Capital Partners, the property is headed to auction.

Netflix had been in talks to buy the 55-acre Studio City lot from Goldman Sachs-led lenders for as much as $400 million, a fraction of the $1.85 billion Hackman paid for it in 2021. The deal was expected to close earlier this year, though the deadline passed without a sale.

Now, Radford is going on the block. A foreclosure auction is scheduled for Nov. 24 in Pomona, according to a notice recorded in Los Angeles County. The lenders are looking for an estimated $1.3 billion — roughly the amount of debt tied to the property — though the final purchase price will likely come in far below that figure as production levels in Los Angeles hover around historic lows.

The expectation is for Netflix to come out of the auction as the top bidder, giving the entertainment giant ownership of a major Los Angeles production campus.

“The deal is progressing on the agreed upon timetable and with the agreed upon sets of milestone dates,” says a Netflix spokesperson.

The purchase will shake up Netflix’s production footprint in Los Angeles. For years, it’s been the anchor tenant at Sunset Studios, owned by Hudson Pacific Properties, while also filming at Raleigh Studios. With Radford, Netflix could consolidate production scattered across the region while cutting costs associated with renting by becoming an owner of a sprawling shooting campus.

Heading into the auction later this month, Netflix is poised to acquire Radford at a generational discount. The reported $400 million price point would be roughly 22 percent of the $1.85 billion Hackman Capital paid for it in 2021, a massive repricing of a legacy Hollywood lot and indicative of the flight of filming away from the region.

“It’s a done deal,” says a person with knowledge of the situation.

Netflix asked Goldman to handle the foreclosure and associated costs, says a source familiar with the talks, and facilitate a sale. A consideration was the so-called mansion tax, which imposes a 5.5 percent levy for properties valued above $10.9 million, according to the source. Here, that could’ve been roughly $22 million.

“There are a number of reasons a deal would be structured in this fashion that have nothing to do with taxation,” says a source familiar with the negotiations.

If Netflix had bought Radford from the lenders, it would’ve had to manage the foreclosure process, potentially adding time and uncertainty before it could take control of the property.

Still, a competing bidder could emerge during the auction that drives the price above the reported $400 million Netflix was considering. Private equity looking to buy a distressed asset or institutional real estate investors could come into play, though the number of entities with the appetite to take on a production campus in L.A. as filming levels continue to plunge is believed to be limited.

A Radford purchase will also have an impact on Netflix’s office operations, though the property can’t fulfill all of the company’s office space needs. For years, Netflix has leased the ICON, EPIC and CUE buildings at Sunset Studios.

Cushman & Wakefield is marketing a loan, led by Mike Condon Jr. and Kevin Donner, secured by Netflix’s animation office on Vine Street., a roughly 95,000-square-foot campus owned by Clarion Partners. The property is fully leased to Netflix through January 2031, with $23.8 million in remaining rent, according to the offering.

The offering is for the debt, not the property itself. But the marketing of a loan secured by a building whose sole tenant is Netflix, who’s under contract for several more years, could be an early sign of uncertainty surrounding the company’s longer-term tenancy plans.

There’s no indication that Netflix plans to vacate the Vine Street campus. Still, the timing is notable: the lease expires in January 2031, just months before Netflix’s leases across three Hudson Pacific Properties buildings — EPIC, ICON and CUE — are scheduled to expire in September 2031. The property doesn’t appear to be on sublease markets.

“Is this next?” says the source, who notes that the loan offering is “unusual” considering the timing.

Another person close to Netflix says that the company has “not had any conversations with the landlord regarding a change in the lease at Vine.”

Since 2018, Netflix has filmed more than 300 movies and TV shows primarily in L.A.

“Los Angeles is an incredibly important place for film and television production, and we’re committed to keeping it one of our core production hubs in the US — supporting the city and the creative community that makes it such a vibrant place to work,” it said in a press release earlier this year. “With its diverse locations, deep bench of talent, experienced crews, best-in-class vendors and a wide variety of locations, the city offers everything we need to bring ambitious stories to life.”

#712. Yella Beezy Found Guilty in 2020 Murder of Rapper MO3 on a Dallas Highway

The 35-year-old was unanimously convicted of capital murder.

Yella Beezy (born Markies Conway) was convicted on capital murder charges by a Dallas County jury on Wednesday (Nov. 11) for hiring the gunman who shot and killed rapper MO3 (born Melvin Noble).

Beezy was sentenced to life in prison without the chance for parole, according to the Associated Press.

“We don’t know what turned it for the jurors. We appreciate the verdict,” lead prosecutor Tommy Adams said. “We think they got it right today. It’s been one of the most challenging cases over the last six years.”

Beezy affiliate Kewon White was found guilty of capital murder and sentenced to life in prison without parole. Prosecutors painted White as the gunman who killed MO3 on a Dallas interstate in November 2020.

White pulled up alongside MO3’s vehicle on I-35 in South Dallas near the Dallas Zoo, which led to him chasing the rival rapper on foot and firing more than 40 rounds from a pistol.

MO3 was transported to a local hospital, but succumbed to his injuries. White was allegedly paid $40,000 by Beezy to gun down the “Everybody” rapper.

“This is capital murder, and the state has brought you a lot of speculation,” Yella Beezy’s attorney John Gussio told the courtroom.

The gallery was emotional as the guilty verdict was read, as Beezy’s family and friends wept and exchanged hugs. CBS News footage showed Beezy asking to kiss a family member — a request that appeared to be denied — before being escorted out of the courtroom.

Yella Beezy was indicted by a Dallas grand jury and arrested in March 2025. He secured a $750,000 bond less than two weeks later after the bond was reduced from $2 million.

Beezy was previously arrested in 2021 on charges of sexual assault, abandonment of an endangered child and unlawful weapon carrying, but they were all dismissed.

The 35-year-old was the victim of a drive-by shooting in October 2018 in a Dallas suburb, but survived after being shot three times.

On the music front, Yella Beezy notched a pair of Billboard Hot 100 hits with “That’s On Me,” which peaked at No. 56 in 2018 and “Bacc at It Again” alongside Quavo and Gucci Mane in 2019 (No. 78 peak). He’s released a handful of singles in 2026, including “Where I Been,” “Let Me Vent” and “Sweet Nothings” with K Camp.
