#711. Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth

For nearly a century, scientists have considered the possibility that comets helped make life on Earth possible by delivering essential organic molecules from space. Now, new research suggests this long-standing explanation is extremely unlikely.

Comets are known to contain many of the chemical compounds associated with the origins of life. These substances, often called prebiotic molecules, can participate in the chemical reactions that eventually produce the complex ingredients needed for living organisms. For decades, researchers have proposed that comets striking the early Earth supplied a steady stream of these compounds.

However, a new study led by the University of Cambridge challenges that theory. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers found that comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make it extremely difficult for delicate organic molecules to survive. Instead of delivering their chemical cargo intact, most would likely destroy it during their violent arrival.

The findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest that successful delivery of life's building blocks by comets would have been an extraordinarily rare event. Interestingly, the researchers also found that Mars may have offered somewhat better conditions for receiving these molecules, although the likelihood remains very low.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get out of jail free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge's Institute of Astronomy. "It's kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it's highly unlikely."

Why Comets May Have Failed to Deliver Life's Building Blocks

The idea that comets could transport the ingredients for life received renewed attention in 2023, when Anslow and several colleagues explored how these icy objects might behave in planetary systems where worlds orbit relatively close together.

Their earlier research suggested that comets could potentially lose speed as they passed between neighboring planets. Through a series of gravitational encounters, a comet might effectively bounce from one planet to another, eventually traveling slowly enough to deliver organic molecules without destroying them.

The team wanted to determine whether a similar process could have occurred in our own Solar System, potentially explaining how essential chemicals reached the young Earth.

"We're learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century," he said.

To investigate, the researchers combined several sophisticated modeling techniques. These included simulations of comet impacts, calculations of how comets interact with planetary atmospheres, and models tracing how comet populations formed and changed as the Solar System developed.

The results revealed a major obstacle. Although a comet might occasionally approach Earth under conditions favorable for preserving organic compounds, such encounters would have been exceptionally uncommon. Successful delivery could not be completely ruled out, but the simulations indicated that it was highly improbable.

A Critical Ingredient for Life Faces Nearly Impossible Odds

To better understand what happens to the molecules carried by comets, the team concentrated on hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a chemical commonly detected in comets throughout our Solar System.

Despite its reputation as a highly toxic substance, hydrogen cyanide is important in research on the origins of life. It contains carbon and nitrogen and can participate in reactions that produce more complex organic compounds, making it a potentially valuable ingredient in the chemistry that preceded living organisms.

The simulations showed that even when hydrogen cyanide managed to survive a comet's arrival, another major problem remained. The impact would need to deposit enough of the molecule in one location to support meaningful chemical reactions. Events capable of producing those useful concentrations were extraordinarily rare.

Timing created yet another difficulty. Comet impacts were much more common during Earth's earliest history, but their frequency declined sharply over the planet's first 500 million years. According to the researchers, there may have been only a handful of opportunities during that entire early period for comets to deliver hydrogen cyanide under favorable conditions.

Even a successful delivery would not necessarily have helped life develop. Hydrogen cyanide deposited on Earth's surface would likely have dispersed or become diluted relatively quickly, leaving little time for the chemical reactions associated with life's origins to get underway.

For the comet theory to work, several unlikely events would therefore have needed to occur together. A comet would have had to strike at just the right speed and angle, preserve its organic cargo, deposit enough material in a suitable location, and trigger important chemical processes before those molecules dispersed.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can't rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence - at best, a one-off fluke."

If Not Comets, Where Did Life's Ingredients Come From?

The findings raise a fundamental question about Earth's earliest history. If comets were unlikely to supply the chemical building blocks of life, what was responsible?

One possibility involves asteroids, which collided with the early Earth far more frequently than comets. The researchers suggest that asteroid impacts could have created conditions in which important prebiotic molecules formed through chemical reactions associated with those collisions.

Another explanation is that Earth produced these compounds on its own. Natural chemical processes operating on the young planet may have generated the ingredients necessary for increasingly complex chemistry, without requiring organic molecules to arrive from space.

These possibilities do not establish exactly how life began. Instead, they highlight alternative ways that the raw materials for life could have become available on Earth.

Why Mars May Have Had a Better Chance Than Earth

While the simulations cast serious doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, they also revealed an intriguing possibility involving Mars.

The Red Planet is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere. These characteristics make it a potentially more favorable destination for cometary molecules, since incoming objects could be more likely to reach its surface without completely destroying their chemical cargo.

According to the researchers, Mars may therefore have been better positioned to receive prebiotic compounds during the Solar System's early development, when comet encounters were considerably more frequent.

However, the simulations do not demonstrate that such deliveries actually occurred. Even on Mars, the conditions required for a successful transfer of life's chemical ingredients appear difficult to achieve.

"This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn't happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn't happen on either planet."

What the Discovery Means for the Search for Alien Life

Beyond changing how scientists think about Earth's early chemistry, the findings could help guide the search for potentially habitable planets in other star systems.

Future space observatories may be able to investigate distant worlds in greater detail, searching for atmospheric clues that could indicate environments suitable for life. Among the proposed missions is the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a potential successor to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The researchers suggest that planetary systems where comets can move between closely spaced planets while gradually losing speed may deserve particular attention. In such environments, the unusual comet delivery mechanism explored in their earlier research could be more likely to operate.

Identifying these systems could help astronomers focus future observations on planets where essential organic molecules may have had a better chance of surviving their journey through space.

Although the new findings make comets an unlikely explanation for how life's building blocks reached Earth, they do not eliminate the possibility that cometary delivery played a role elsewhere. Understanding where these chemical transfers are possible could provide valuable clues as scientists continue investigating how life emerges across the universe.

The research received partial support from the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), which is part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

#710. Randall England, ‘General Hospital’ Actor, Dies at 75

He played the villainous Jack Slater on the ABC soap opera and, later, Bill Clinton on the stage.

Randall England, who portrayed Jack Slater, a villain fond of red cowboy boots, for eight months in the mid-1980s on the ABC soap General Hospital, has died. He was 75.

England died Sept. 25 after a battle with esophageal cancer, his family announced. He lived in Beverly Hills for more than 40 years, and the town “won’t be the same without him cruising around in his vintage BMW, sporting his dark Ray-Ban sunglasses,” they noted.

From November 1984 through June 1985, England played Slater, a killer and jewel thief who went toe-to-toe with Tristan Rogers’ Robert Scorpio before he’s shot to death. (It turns out he was a fan of cowboy boots in real life.) Related Stories Movies Irma P. Hall, Actress in 'Soul Food' and 'The Ladykillers,' Dies at 91 Movies Stacy Keach, Who Played Badasses With the Best of Them, Dies at 85

One of three kids, Randy Alan England was born in Oklahoma City on Sept. 22, 1951. He graduated from Memorial High School and the University of Oklahoma, where he was a pitcher for the Sooners.

After working as a model on gigs that took him to London, Zurich, Milan and Los Angeles, he studied acting in the late 1970s and early ’80s with Kim Stanley and Stella Adler. An audition brought him to L.A., and in 1981 he showed up as a model in the Michael Crichton thriller Looker, starring Albert Finney.

England also appeared on episodes of Dallas, The Young and the Restless and Baywatch and in the 2015 music video for Maroon 5’s “Sugar.”

For the stage, he played President Clinton in Hillary & Monica in 2003 in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, and acted in productions of All My Sons, The Glass Menagerie and Three Sisters.

He was working on documentary that honored Stanley’s life and career and the time of his death.

Survivors include his daughter, Micaela, and son-in-law, Sam; his grandchildren, Katherine and Julian; his mother, Catherine; sister Linda; nieces and nephews Amanda, Wesley and Alex; and ex-wife Jennifer.

Donations in his memory can be made to the Esophageal Cancer Action Network.

With comets out of the picture, attention now turns to asteroids or even Earth itself as the source of prebiotic chemistry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet.

Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth.

Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement.

Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets.For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely.

Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves.

In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.

The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second).Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."

It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet.

However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth.

Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA.

However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars, because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity."This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet."

More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1, where all the planets are bunched up close.

In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive.

The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports.

#708. A mysterious 93-billion-mile cosmic structure may be the wreckage of colliding worlds

A mysterious structure stretching roughly 93 billion miles across space is giving astronomers new clues about the violent events that shape young planetary systems. Known as the "Cat's Tail," this enormous cloud of dark material lies about 63 light-years from Earth, in the faint constellation Pictor (which is Latin for "painter"). For the past two years, its unusual appearance and uncertain origins have puzzled scientists.

The structure is part of a vast disk of dust and debris surrounding Beta Pictoris, a young star system that resembles our own solar system during its early development. Now, using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have captured previously hidden details of the Cat's Tail in visible light for the first time.

The discovery is described in a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Led by University of Arizona planetary scientist Arin Avsar, the research team combined the new Hubble images with observations spanning more than 14 years. Their findings provide a clearer picture of the structure's composition, location, and shape, along with additional evidence that a massive collision may have created it.

A Possible Collision Between Pluto-Sized Worlds

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies - think something like Pluto," said Avsar, a doctoral student working with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory.

"Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

The mystery becomes even more interesting when viewed in the context of how planetary systems form.

Today, our solar system appears relatively orderly. Planets follow established paths around the Sun, while many smaller rocky objects occupy "designated" regions such as the asteroid belt. But 4.6 billion years ago, the situation was dramatically different.

A young sun was surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust. Rocky objects repeatedly collided, sometimes breaking apart and sometimes combining into larger bodies. Over time, some accumulated enough material to become planets, while countless others were destroyed or scattered.

Astronomers study younger systems like Beta Pictoris because they offer an opportunity to observe processes that unfolded in our own cosmic neighborhood billions of years ago. Its debris disk, consisting of dust and fragments left behind during planetary development, is believed to be approaching the final stages of planet formation.

Why Hubble Could Finally See the Mysterious Cat's Tail

One of the most intriguing questions about the Cat's Tail is why it was previously detectable in infrared light but so difficult to observe in visible light.

The answer may lie in the unusual material that makes up the enormous structure.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

Organic refractory material consists of complex carbon compounds that can withstand relatively harsh conditions in space. Because these compounds absorb much of the visible light that strikes them, they can make the surrounding dust appear exceptionally dark.

The Hubble observations also support another unusual finding: the Cat's Tail appears to be composed of extremely small, surprisingly porous dust particles.

Individual grains measure only about a micron across, roughly one millionth of a meter. Yet instead of being compact and solid, they appear remarkably "fluffy," with substantial empty space within their structures.

The scale of the entire cloud is difficult to imagine. It may stretch as far as 1,000 astronomical units, with one astronomical unit (AU) defined as the average distance between Earth and the Sun. That corresponds to approximately 93 billion miles, or the equivalent of lining up around 200 trillion house cats from tail to nose.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

How a Violent Collision Could Create Fluffy Cosmic Dust

If the Cat's Tail really formed when large planetary bodies smashed into each other, researchers still need to explain how that destruction produced such tiny, porous particles.

One possibility is that the collision was powerful enough to vaporize some of the material involved.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," said co-author Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory.

In this scenario, the intense impact would have transformed solid carbon material into gas. As the material cooled, it could have condensed back into solid particles with unusually open, lightweight structures.

However, the precise process remains uncertain, and additional observations will be needed to determine whether this explanation is correct.

A 93-Billion-Mile Structure With an Unexpected Shape

The new research also challenges previous assumptions about where the Cat's Tail extends in space.

By combining visible light observations from Hubble with infrared measurements from the James Webb Space Telescope, the researchers used computer modeling to reconstruct the structure's possible three-dimensional arrangement.

Earlier observations suggested that the Cat's Tail extended outward from Beta Pictoris and far behind the star from Earth's perspective. Because the surrounding debris disk is viewed nearly edge-on, it was difficult to determine how much of the structure extended away from us rather than across our field of view.

The new analysis points to a different explanation.

"We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat's Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it," Avsar said. "It's essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it."

This suggests the structure may be spread mainly across the sky as seen from Earth, rather than projecting deep into space behind the star.

The revised geometry gives astronomers a better understanding of where the dust is located and could help them reconstruct the event that produced it.

Hubble Discovers a Strange Warp Caused by a Giant Planet

The Cat's Tail was not the only unusual feature revealed by the new observations.

Using Hubble in a different observational configuration, Avsar and his colleagues also identified an unexpected distortion in the broad halo of dust surrounding Beta Pictoris.

The researchers suspect this strange warp may be caused by the gravitational influence of Beta Pic b, one of three planets in the system.

Beta Pic b is a massive gas giant estimated to be about 10 times the mass of Jupiter. Its powerful gravity may be disturbing the surrounding debris, altering the paths of dust particles, comets, and other icy objects across enormous distances.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units."

The finding highlights how giant planets can shape their environments far beyond their immediate orbits.

A Glimpse Into Our Solar System's Violent Past

For researchers, Beta Pictoris offers more than an opportunity to investigate an unusual cosmic structure. It may also provide a window into the early history of our own solar system.

Consider the Kuiper Belt, the distant region beyond Neptune that contains Pluto and numerous other icy bodies.

When the Kuiper Belt was only about 20 million years old, astronomers believe it was much more crowded than it is today. It may have contained hundreds of objects comparable in size to Pluto.

Over billions of years, the gravitational influence of the solar system's outer giant planets likely changed that environment dramatically. By disturbing the orbits of smaller bodies, these planets may have pushed many objects into new regions or expelled them from the solar system entirely, effectively "clearing out" much of the original population.

The strange dust tail and newly identified warp around Beta Pictoris may offer clues to similar processes unfolding in another planetary system.

By studying these distant structures, astronomers hope to better understand how violent collisions, migrating debris, and the immense gravity of giant planets helped transform the chaos of the early solar system into the planetary arrangement we see today.

#707. China’s Film Industry Arrives at AFM on a Domestic High

Revenue still trails last year’s 'Ne Zha 2'-fueled peak, but homegrown hits are driving the 2026 box office and the industry is courting partners abroad.

Chinese filmmaker Wen Muye keeps taking what look on paper like challenging subjects and turning them into box office gold.

It began with his 2018 debut, Dying to Survive, about a man (Xu Zheng) who makes a fortune smuggling cancer drugs into China. The film took in more than $450 million, and Wen was hailed as an exciting new voice in Chinese cinema. He blended so much humanity and humor into the story that, by the time the credits rolled, the film had become the tale of a man who went looking for cash but found his soul.

When news of Wen’s latest venture broke, Chinese media initially struggled with what they’d heard of Once Upon a Time in the Middle East: the fact that it would be set in the war-torn Middle East, inside a Chinese restaurant, and would star one of the country’s most beloved comedians in Shen Teng (Pegasus) led to some head scratching. Related Stories Movies Can Constantin Survive Its Own Parent Company? Movies Magnolia Pictures Takes French Animated Gay Comedy 'Jim Queen' for U.S.

But, again, Wen has worked his magic. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East became a $360 million-odd hit at home, thanks in no small part to the filmmaker’s talent for mixing genres, with warm humor to be found along with moments of dramatic devastation, and what might well be a career-defining turn from Shen. Again, as with Wen’s first feature, it’s the tale of an everyman turned hero.

The director points to three key ingredients when he was writing the script and working on the ways in which he would present the movie to the world: Wen says he was looking to combine “entertainment value” with “social relevance” and “soulfulness.” To do that, he presents an assortment of relatable characters, drawn together through circumstance and held together by their shared humanity.

“Even if the audience does not usually think about big questions, after watching it, would they be willing to think about things like war and peace, hope and human relationships?” begins Wen. “These three levels go deeper and deeper. It is already not easy to achieve entertainment value. [But] if one can also enter social relevance and finally leave a longer spiritual memory, that is of course the state I hope for.”

Wen’s film has become one of the biggest success stories in the world’s second-largest film market, and it’s now the country’s official submission in the international Oscar category. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East is also down for one of four market screenings being hosted at AFM by the China Film Pavilion, an initiative staged under the guidance of China Film Administration, hosted by the China Film Co-production Corporation (CFCC) and back at the market for the fourth year in a row.

Those screenings reflect the recent move toward a more varied output from the Chinese film industry. Alongside the star vehicle that is Once Upon a Time in the Middle East comes the Lan Hongchun-directed box office smash Dear You ($300 million) — a gentle but sweeping family drama — as well as the animated hit Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector, the 12th release in the blockbuster franchise that has taken in more than $1 billion in China alone. Rounding out the CFCC’s AFM slate is the documentary Daughter of the River, drawn from the memoirs of acclaimed author Hong Ying and tracing the lives of generations of women living in the southwestern city of Chongqing.

This year’s China Film Pavilion has showcased 70 film companies and institutions, among them the China Film Group Corporation, CMC Pictures, Lianray Pictures, China Film Archive, China Film Foundation and the Shanghai International Film Festival. As well as market screenings (held at MC Century City), the on-site AFM facility has been promoting more than 200 titles, among them the much-anticipated sci-fi epic The Wandering Earth 3 — a franchise that has so far collected roughly $1.3 billion — the Jiang Xuanyi-helmed actioner Brotherhood of Blades 3 and the animated fantasy hit All Wishes Come True!

Other initiatives this year include a mixer on Nov. 11 at which leading Chinese industry figures will discuss the state of their domestic scene while showcasing more films. There will also be a main-market, CFCC-hosted seminar titled “Beyond Co-Production: New Models for Financing, Creating, and Distributing Global Screen IP” that focuses on four issues: “how to combine financing, talent and production resources from different countries; how to incorporate global distribution and audience considerations from the project planning stage; how AI can reduce production costs while preserving creators’ unique styles; and how to carry out cross-cultural redevelopment of classic films and established IP.”

The session is moderated by Rance Pow, founder and CEO at Artisan Gateway — the Los Angeles-based consulting firm that offers analysis of the Chinese film industry — and features as panelists Apelles Entertainment founder Belle Avery; executive vp and head of corporate banking at East West Bank Bennett Pozil; founder and CEO at Leeding Media David Lee; senior global entertainment executive at U.S. China Co-Productions Randy Greenberg; and William Feng, who’s head of Greater China and vp at the Motion Picture Association Asia Pacific.

The aim, according to the CFCC, is to explore “new avenues for global cooperation” and to “facilitate international film transactions, solidify Sino-foreign cinematic partnerships and boost cultural appreciation within the global industry.”

The Chinese industry arrives for AFM boosted by a run of successful local hits in 2026 and some positive box office news. By the end of October, revenue had topped $4.7 billion, with more than 800 million admissions and roughly 122 million screenings, according to state-run media reports. Year-on-year, China is still down around 29 percent — with the caveat that 2025 was bumped by the freakish success of the animated hit Ne Zha 2, which took in a staggering $2.2 billion. But what seems to be driving optimism is the fact that 2026’s overall box office is mostly being driven by domestic releases.

By October’s end, eight of the country’s top 10 films for the year were local, led by the action-comedy Pegasus 3 ($656 million) and followed by Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.

Wen’s own explanation for his film’s success is more straightforward. He puts it down to the fact that, on so many levels, the characters and the conversations they have are so relatable.

“I have always been interested in the state of ordinary people in specific environments, because ordinary people are not making big choices every day,” says Wen. “Most of the time, they are dealing with very concrete things like eating, work, family, money and relationships. But when circumstances truly push them into a certain position, they may also do things they could not normally do. For me, this change is not about first writing a hero and then adding an ordinary person’s life to him. It is about starting from an ordinary person and seeing how far he can go under the pressure of reality.”

#706. ‘The Odyssey’ Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs

Matt Damon moderated a crew Q&A after the premiere of Christopher Nolan’s 75-minute making-of documentary.

That was my first thought after watching “Behind the Scenes of ‘The Odyssey,’” a 75-minute documentary chronicling the making of Christopher Nolan’s $1.8 billion blockbuster, which premiered Tuesday night at the Spielberg Theater on the Universal Studios lot.

“I have absolutely mastered the art of talking a lot and revealing absolutely nothing,” Nolan joked as he introduced the film. “And so I’m told I need to get out of the way.” Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings

Most viewers won’t see the full version screened Tuesday. The 75-minute cut was a one-time presentation, while a shorter version will be included with the film’s digital home release, arriving Nov. 17. Universal has not announced which portions will make the cut.

After the screening, star Matt Damon, who plays Odysseus, moderated an hourlong conversation with 12 department heads: producer Emma Thomas, production designer Ruth De Jong, editor Jennifer Lame, composer and songwriter Ludwig Göransson, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, special effects supervisor Scott Fisher, costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, casting director John Papsidera, supervising sound editor Craig Henighan, production sound mixer Willie Burton, head of makeup Luisa Abel and head of hair Gloria Casny.

The room was packed with guild voters and social media influencers, including comedian and actor Evan M. Williams. Afterward, the crowd spilled into the lobby, where exhibits on the film’s artisan achievements awaited and multiple conversations and selfies began.

The premiere kicks off two weeks of Universal awards-season screenings for “The Odyssey,” the highest-grossing film of Nolan’s career. The studio is campaigning the film across all categories, aiming to match or break the record 16 Oscar nominations Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners” earned earlier this year.

The campaign continues Wednesday, when Robert Downey Jr. moderates an Imax 70mm screening at the TCL Chinese Theatre, followed Thursday by Guillermo del Toro at AMC Universal CityWalk. On Nov. 17, Steven Spielberg sits down with Nolan at the DGA Theater, the same day “The Odyssey” arrives on digital.

Nolan is also paying it forward Saturday, moderating a Q&A with “Digger” director Alejandro G. Iñárritu.

Here are eight of the most revealing moments from the documentary and the Q&A.

Matt Damon didn’t loop a single line on “The Odyssey”

Damon revealed that he did not have to re-record a single line of dialogue for “The Odyssey,” a rarity for a production of this scale. “I did not loop a line for this movie,” he said onstage, turning to legendary production sound mixer Burton to ask how he pulled it off.

Burton explained Nolan’s strict rules. “There’s no ADR with Chris,” he said. “Does not want to do ADR, and he also wants the boom mic to be on a cable.”

The commitment to capturing sound on set extended to the ship itself. Burton recalled being sent below deck during the production, where he ran cables under the floorboards and mounted microphones on the hull. During storm sequences, water poured down on him. He also became the ship’s unofficial snack clerk.

“I’m trying to do sound now, and one of the guys is, ‘Can you hand me potato chips?’” Burton recalled getting boisterous laughter from the crowd.

The documentary also shows how much attention went into the film’s sound design. Henighan sent a crew to record the ship for real, including every oar stroke. Re-recording mixers Gary Rizzo and Kevin O’Connell note that nearly everything in the mix is organic, from gongs forged by human hands to the army’s actual screams.

Nolan wanted nothing to do with the “very cartoony, very unthreatening” Cyclops sequences of decades past. His visual inspiration was Francisco Goya’s “Saturn Devouring His Son,” particularly its blank, indifferent face.

De Jong suggested turning the creature’s single eye sideways and centering it. Jackson then conducted a simple test: He filmed actor Bill Irwin, who plays Polyphemus, improvising in a dark Universal office with a desk lamp on the floor. Jackson digitally moved one of Irwin’s eyes to the center of his face and painted out the other.

“It was quite phenomenal, actually, how effective it was,” Jackson said.

The documentary also reveals that the giant creature was initially represented by a crude stick-figure puppet. The original plan was to shoot the sequence on an L.A. soundstage late in production. But after Nolan and De Jong scouted Greece and found a real cave, the team had to finish the puppet and get it standing on a Greek mountain within two months.

The production ultimately built only the creature’s rigid parts around the simpler structure. “Because of the way that we were forced to make it in a much simpler way, it actually worked much better,” he said.

Tom Holland asked for a shorter skirt to look taller, and Robert Pattinson wanted a long wig. Both were rejected by Nolan.

Thomas, Nolan’s producing partner and wife, described two versions of the director: one who demands the impossible during preparation and another who becomes “incredibly pragmatic” once shooting starts.

The documentary offers a running list of things Nolan won’t allow.

Marking her first Nolan film, Casny received a request from Robert Pattinson, who plays Antinous, for a long wig. The actor called her on the first day of fittings while she was standing next to Nolan and Thomas. “I didn’t even know how he got my number,” Casny recalled. “The answer was no.”

Holland tells a story in the documentary about his first costume fitting, where he quietly asked Mirojnick to shorten his skirt a bit so he’d look taller. Six weeks later, the alteration was done and the costume went before Nolan. “Two seconds into taking in the costume, he was like, ‘How come the skirt is shorter?’” Holland says.

Nolan’s attention to detail is paramount which Damon even chimed in to highlight. He recalled a day on “Oppenheimer” when a missing hat delayed the company on a moving train for half an hour. Thomas jumped in with the obvious lesson learned: “He does not like hats.”

And when Henighan presented a particularly graphic, squelchy sound design for the Samantha Morton’s Circe sequence, Nolan wasn’t interested. He preferred dry bones cracking and knuckles popping.

Nolan told his Marine Coordinator, ‘I Don’t Accept That’ about physics.

Damon recalled a moment in Scotland when the sea tore apart one of the production’s boats during the Laestrygonian sequence. Marine coordinator Neil Andrea explained that the transom and hull had been ripped out and that getting the vessel ready for the next day was “literally impossible.”

“And Chris turned to Neil and said, ‘I don’t accept that,’” Damon recalled. “And somehow that thing was floating the next day, and we shot on it.”

Thomas, gamely defending her husband, added: “I promise you, he’s more pragmatic than that.”

The sea was the production’s most stubborn adversary. Nolan admitted that he had privately hoped to minimize boat time while writing the script. “But it’s ‘The Odyssey,’” he said. “Of course, we’re going to be on this boat for months.”

Andrea’s team converted Viking ship replicas from Scandinavia into Greek warships, hiding small engines inside them. The storm destruction sequences were eventually filmed on the Universal backlot, with jet engines blasting the ship on a gimbal.

The production’s logistical challenges extended to the Trojan horse itself. In Morocco, Nolan moved the start date up two days while the enormous prop was still sitting in crates at customs.

“I’m like, ‘What? The horse is in boxes in customs.’ And he’s like, ‘Yeah, anyways, carry on,’” De Jong recalled.

When the crew finally planted the horse in the sand for the opening shot, the incoming tide knocked it over. Nolan’s response? “Great. Well, I’m gonna shoot this tomorrow.”

The fall of Troy was built practically, with a 2.5-acre city constructed between late December and early February. Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema wanted to light the entire film with fire, so he designed hundreds of LED fixtures, nicknamed “pyrahedrons,” calibrated to the color of firelight.

Nolan sees his entire filmography inside Homer

The documentary’s opening stretch plays like a Nolan master class, with Damon recalling the conversation that started the project. Nolan caught up with him for 10 or 15 minutes and said two words: “The Odyssey.”

Nolan describes Homer’s poem as containing all of Western literature, including the DNA of his own films. Adapting it meant recognizing “that’s where I got that thing from ‘Interstellar,’ or that’s where ‘The Dark Knight’ comes from.”

Rather than imitate the Romantic-era paintings and Hollywood epics of the 1950s and ’60s that defined the genre, Nolan applied the grounded approach of “The Dark Knight,” “Inception” and “Interstellar” to Greek mythology.

Ludwig Göransson built the score around 35 bronze gongs

Damon said that whenever he asked what Göransson was working on, Nolan answered with one word: gongs.

The composer explained that he shut himself in his studio during the Los Angeles fires, surrounded by about 35 bronze gongs and spent 10 days learning to write for them. He had heard gongs before, he noted, “in the theme song for ‘Mortal Kombat.’”

From there, Göransson sought out musicians who played the ancient aulos and lyre. He also traveled to southern Albania to record iso-polyphonic folk singing.

The documentary’s music chapter ends at Abbey Road with vocalist James Blake. The end-credits song, “When I’m Home,” came about because Göransson wanted the film to finish the song started by the bard, played by Travis Scott. The track uses Scott’s original vocal recording from the movie.

Nearly 7,000 extras were put through hair and makeup and Matt Damon performs pullups.

The documentary makes clear that grounding Greek mythology in reality required enormous detail. More than 80 hair and makeup artists worked in Morocco, and just under 7,000 background performers passed through fittings.

The teams erased every modern tell, from tattoos and earring holes to the shape of women’s eyebrows.

Mirojnick also created distinct visual identities for the principal characters.

Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, wears bright colors because, as the actress explains, she isn’t a widow and keeps dressing as if her husband will return. Telemachus (Tom Holland) transitions from boy to man through increasingly bright, light armor, while Antinous wears a leopard pelt.

As for casting, Papsidera says Nolan once described Homer as writing “the Marvel films of his time,” so the actors had to be the superstars of ours. Odysseus’ warriors, though, needed real bodies. “You don’t want it to look like, you know, 2025 bodybuilding,” Papsidera says. “They weren’t taking peptides.”

Papsidera, whose work ends before cameras roll, had his doubts. “This pragmatic Chris, I’d like to meet sometime,” he cracked, adding that he doesn’t even get a copy of the script to keep. He also joked with Damon of the pecking order: “No movie without us, buddy.”

And most notably, points to the short prep time that left him roughly 62 days to cast about 60 actors.

Damon, meanwhile, was well aware of the physical demands of playing Odysseus. Filmed doing pullups on a ladder, the actor offers a candid assessment of the production. “I’m 54 years old, and I knew this was going to be really physical.”

Near the end of the doc, Damon delivers the line that may become the campaign’s rallying cry. “My whole life was kind of leading up to this movie, and I don’t know how long we’re going to get to make movies this way.”

Onstage, Thomas turned the spotlight on the moderator, making sure voters know the movie couldn’t exist without its star, who has yet to win an acting Oscar. “I cannot believe we did it,” she said, crediting Damon for being “on set, on time with the best attitude every morning.”

Damon passed the praise back down the row. “I’ve never seen more asked of a crew, never,” Damon concluded. “And I don’t think I ever could again.” Then he pauses chuckling. “That didn’t come out right.”

#705. Jessica Chastain to Star on Broadway in ‘Lost Lear’

Michael Urie and Corey Stoll will also star in the play at the Booth Theatre this spring.

Jessica Chastain has confirmed her return to Broadway in the new play Lost Lear.

The play, written and directed by Dan Colley, follows a former actress with dementia who imagines she’s back in rehearsal for King Lear. Corey Stoll will star as her estranged son, with Michael Urie starring as her nurse, stepping into various roles in the play.

Chastain returns to Broadway after starring in the 2023 Broadway revival of A Doll’s House. The Academy Award winner teased the return on the Today show last week, while promoting her new Netflix film Heartland.

The play is set to begin performances at the Booth Theatre on March 29, with an opening night on April 23. It comes to Broadway after premiering at Dublin Theatre Festival in 2022 and touring the U.S., U.K. and New Zealand. The play won the Scotsman Fringe First award at Edinburgh Festival Fringe in 2025.

“I never imagined, when we first made Lost Lear, that it would one day be on Broadway – and I’ve imagined some pretty wild things,” Colley said. “I’m so thrilled to have the opportunity to share this piece with New York audiences and to discover new facets of the work through collaborating with this remarkable company of artists.”

Urie, who stars as Brian in Apple TV+’s Shrinking, most recently appeared on Broadway in Oh, Mary! after a long list of Broadway credits including the 2024 revival of Once Upon a Mattress, Spamalot and the revival of Harvey Fierstein’s Torch Song.

Stoll, also known for his role as Peter on House Of Cards, among many onscreen appearances, returns to Broadway after being Tony nominated for his role in the 2024 revival of Appropriate.

Seaview, MarketStall and Mass Productions with Pam Hurst-Della Pietra & Stephen Della Pietra are producing. Additional casting will be announced at a later date.

#703. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy, astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere.

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much. At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth. This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed.

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Alix is an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham specialising in the characterisation of stars and exoplanets. She is passionate about science communication, and how astrophysics is portrayed in movies, TV, and pop culture at large.

#701. Iconic first image of black hole holds up to scrutiny

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). Physicists used an algorithm to combine telescope measurements of a black hole in a different way to the original analysis.Credit: S. Lai, N. Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong, and F. Diakogiannis; Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration wowed the world in 2019 with the first picture ever taken of a black hole’s shadow. Some researchers were unconvinced, arguing that the circular shape seen in that shot was an artefact of the team’s image-reconstruction techniques. Now, an independent group has reanalysed the EHT data, and its results, published on 11 November in Nature — including new images of the black hole — largely corroborate the original findings1.

To image black holes, the international EHT collaboration stitches together data it collects simultaneously from an array of ground-based radio telescopes that stretches across several continents. The reconstruction is extremely challenging, but in principle the result is an image with the same level of detail, or resolution, that would be achieved with a single radio dish as wide as Earth.

Although blurry, the EHT shot of a supermassive black hole at the centre of the M87 galaxy was consistent with astrophysical models based on Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes. The image had a bright ring of roughly the correct radius, given what was known about the size of the black hole, with a darker disk at the centre.

However, starting in 20222, Junichiro Makino, an astrophysicist at Kobe University in Japan, and his collaborators began questioning those conclusions. By applying one of the data-analysis techniques the EHT collaboration had used, but with slightly different assumptions, Makino’s team obtained a different result. Their image shows a glob of radio emissions rather than a ring.

#700. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's

Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

"The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused."

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots

As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

"So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

#699. ‘One in a Million’ Filmmaker on the Ethical Dilemma He Faced and Learning to Let His Subject Find Her Own Way

Over a decade, co-directors Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes documented a young Syrian girl named Israa and her family's changing dynamics as refugees in Germany.

For One in a Million filmmakers Jack MacInnes and Itab Azzam, documenting the life of a Syrian refugee family for more than a decade meant confronting a complicated question: What’s the line between documenting the truth and protecting your subject?

That conundrum came to a head when a 14-year-old girl named Israa, whom the married documentarians had been following since the age of 11, when her parents decided to immigrate from Turkey to Germany, revealed that her father, Tarek, had hit her. The disclosure came as a shock, given the close relationship they initially witnessed between the pair. Related Stories SCAD Savannah Film Festival "It's All Cinema!" Directors of 2026's Top Docs on Taking Risks, Interacting With Subjects and the Huge Success of 'You Can See Everything' (Video) Movies 'You Can See Everything' Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards

“In the first part of the film, he really is a heroic father,” MacInnes said during a Q&A following a screening of the documentary at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival on Oct. 29. “It just felt like this moment of the scales falling from our eyes,” he added of the revelation. “Have we been naive? What is happening here?”

When the filmmakers returned to their home base of London, they questioned whether they should continue with the project and ensured Israa had the proper resources available to her. Her mother, Nisreen, pleaded with the duo, saying, “‘Don’t tell anyone. We want to deal with this ourselves,’” MacInnes recalled.

“We were obviously worried,” he explained further. “But it turned out Nisreen did have the courage to act and to tend to and look after her children, which ended up becoming the story.”

When the documentary picks up two years later, Nisreen has left Tarek and is happily raising their four children alone, encouraging other women to leave an unhappy relationship despite the difficulty of being a single parent. “The fact that she emerges from the shadows and finds herself — finds her voice — is such a key part of the story,” MacInnes said. Tarek, on the other hand, is living alone in a refugee camp, unable to face the reality of his actions.

Israa’s status at the time is a bit more complicated: the then-16-year-old newly embracing her Muslim faith and wearing the hijab, as she declares her boyfriend, Mohammed, has helped her find freedom through her religion. It’s a development that initially surprised MacInnes and Azzam, particularly in light of her mother’s transformation, he admitted.

“The real exercise for the second half of the film [was] where we started to look at our own prejudices and our own views and started to think, the dreams we thought were her dreams, how much of that was our dreams for her?” he said.

“It’s one of the reasons, at the end of the film, I loved coming back to [Israa’s] dreams when she came into Germany. She wasn’t saying, ‘I want to be an astronaut; I want to go to university.’ She was saying, ‘I want a home, and I want a bed.’ And that’s when we came to realize that what she had lost was family; her family had fallen apart. She’d lost home, she’d lost stability, she’d lost love,” MacInnes said.

The filmmakers continued following the journey of Israa, now 21, through her marriage to Mohammed, their family’s first visit back to Syria following the fall of President Bashar al-Assad’s regime in 2024 and even Israa’s reconciliation with her father, who, near the end of the film, is finally able to own up to his abuse and is building a new relationship with his daughter as a grandfather to her and Mohammed’s son.

“I was talking to Israa yesterday, and she was saying what she’s found is love. And we thought, if she’s found peace and love in this life she’s chosen, then actually there’s a lot for us to learn from that,” said MacInnes. “We came to a place where we saw what she was getting from her Muslim faith, which was peace and faith, and it’s beautiful, I think.”
