#698. Mary Hager, CBS News Politics and ‘Face the Nation’ Guru, to Retire

Mary Hager, the longtime political-news guru and behind-the-scenes force at CBS News and its Sunday public-affairs program, “Face the Nation,” will retire from the program in January, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Hager informed colleagues at CBS News of her decision on Wednesday, these people say, in order to give the Skydance news division time to search for a replacement. There is no obvious successor for Hager in her producer role at “Nation” at this time, largely because Anne Hsu, who was named the program’s executive producer in 2025, is moving to a new role within CBS News, according to the people familiar with the program. Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings

CBS News declined to make executives available for comment. The media-industry newsletter Status previously reported on her decision. Hager could not be reached for immediate comment.

Hager is seen as a force at CBS News, and has been the guiding presence at “Face the Nation” during the tenures of moderators Bob Schieffer, John Dickerson and Margaret Brennan. She covered nearly every presidential campaign, convention and election night over the past 30 years at CBS News, in capacities that range from embed to anchor producer to executive producer of midterm coverage. She also spent more than 15 years as CBS News chief Washington correspondent Bob Schieffer’s producer.

And while she ran or helped run “Face The Nation” since 2011 as a senior producer, executive producer and senior executive producer, she also served in other capacities. Since 2022, she was also CBS News’ executive editor for politics.

In recent years, Hager placed emphasis on the quality of newsmaker bookings and discussions at “Nation,” in a belief that audiences were growing tired of some of the theatrics at the networks’ Sunday mainstays. “I think Sunday shows are getting further away from spin, and I think we are still doing a better job at kind of what we have always been trying to focus on — what is important for viewers, what the takeaways are, what they can learn, as opposed to putting the boxing gloves on and yelling back and forth,” she told Variety in 2019.

During the coronavirus pandemic, Hager helped transform the program into a reliable forum for medical information, dropping some of the political-news segments and turning instead to a medical expert, Scott Gottlieb, a former FDA commissioner. With Brennan on maternity leave for a few months, and John Dickerson filling in, “Nation” featured Gottlieb so many times that he became one of the most frequent non-journalist guests in the program’s history. At the time only Senator John McCain had been on “Nation” more times overall.

She will leave “Nation” as the show is faring well in the ratings. Season to date as of November 8, “Face The Nation” has won more viewers than either NBC’s “Meet The Press” or ABC’s “This Week.” And while it has lost some viewership compared to last season, the show has seen a surge among viewers between 26 and 54, the demographic coveted most by advertisers — and leads its rivals in that category as well.

Hager’s departure surfaces while the management of CBS News under a new owner, Skydance, has come under scrutiny. Since Skydance took over the company once known as Paramount and appointed Bari Weiss, a former digital entrepreneur and opinion journalist, as editor in chief, a number of prominent anchors and producers have chosen to exit. CBS News has also seen layoffs, with some staffers still mulling over buyout offers.

Hager’s retirement was said to be planned, according to people familiar with the matter, and not due to pressure or differences in vision. Even so, her absence from CBS News will be hard to fill in weeks to come.

#697. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

"Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study."

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected

When Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," said Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing."

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly important because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

Oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," said Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong."

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case."

This finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production."

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

Materials provided by Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#696. ‘VisionQuest’ Creator Terry Matalas Tells All About That Supersized Finale and Post-Credits Surprise

The former 'Picard' showrunner also pays tribute to the late Patrick Stewart in a spoiler-filled chat with THR about the final chapter of the WandaVision trilogy: "All endings need to touch on the beginning."

[This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the finale of VisionQuest, “Forever.”]

For showrunner Terry Matalas, VisionQuest was always going to be a Marvel show about fathers and sons.

When he was tapped a few years ago to redevelop the final chapter of the WandaVision trilogy — taking over from creator Jac Schaeffer, who reportedly stepped away from the project to focus on Agatha All Along, the second installment starring Kathryn Hahn — Matalas received just one clear directive from Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige. The new sequel series had to center on Paul Bettany’s synthezoid Vision and his superpowered son Tommy Maximoff — one of the twin boys he shared with Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen), the Scarlet Witch who ostensibly perished at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. Related Stories TV Streaming Ratings: 'From' Netflix Effects Its Way to Top of the Charts General News "You Shall Not Pass": Gandalf, Black Panther and Deadpool Take to the Streets of France

“We knew Tommy was going to be a part of it, and then I had to ask myself, ‘Who is Vision talking to? He doesn’t have Wanda in this show, and Tommy felt like something you want to get to,’” Matalas explains to The Hollywood Reporter. “So I immediately went to Vision’s father, and specifically Ultron [played by] James Spader. I was so enamored by that last scene in Avengers: Age of Ultron between the two of them and asked myself, ‘Well, what if that was the show?’”

Over the course of eight episodes, the newly resurrected “White Vision” — whose original memories had been locked away by the agency S.W.O.R.D. following his death in Avengers: Infinity War, only to have them unlocked by the Hex-created version of himself in the WandaVision finale before flying away — embarks on a deeply psychological journey of self-discovery. As he grapples with his fractured identity, Vision confronts a philosophical, mirror-image Ultron — his deeply toxic, cynical creator functioning as a dark father figure — and struggles to accept Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica), an orphaned teenager who is the super-powered reincarnation of his and Wanda’s son Tommy.

Though she was credited as an executive producer, Schaeffer was not creatively involved in VisionQuest, wanting to give Matalas and his writers’ room — most of whom had worked with him on Star Trek: Picard — “a blank canvas” to play with. “I called her briefly to thank her and just because I’m such a fan of what she did with WandaVision. I watched every episode of that twice when it came out and then would go on YouTube and dissect every single Easter egg,” Matalas says. “But she was very clear upfront that she didn’t want to share any creative [input].”

The VisionQuest finale, however, still pays tribute to WandaVision and Agatha in more ways than one. The series’ overarching puppet master — revealed to be “The Client,” Virgil Horton (also played by Spader, whose human identity inspired Ultron’s avatar) — holds Vision and the A.I. Jocasta (T’Nia Miller) captive to execute a plot for digital immortality. When Virgil fatally shoots Jocasta, a devastated Ultron murders Virgil and unleashes a lethal nanobot swarm on London. To stop the genocidal A.I., Vision traps them both within a creative WandaVision-style sitcom simulation dubbed UltraVision, forcing Ultron to confront the profound heartbreak of losing Jocasta — the A.I. companion he unwittingly fell for — which ultimately neutralizes the threat and causes both of their systems to collapse.

In the aftermath, Tommy and his twin brother Billy (Joe Locke) — who was last seen in Agatha — work together using their combined powers to successfully bring their father back to life. The finale also features a post-credits scene — not included in the screeners sent out to press — of Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom resurrecting Wanda, who had seemingly been crushed under a mountain amid her grief over losing Vision and their twins at the end of Multiverse of Madness. The Maximoff family reunion is on!

Calling from New York City just hours before the VisionQuest finale dropped on Disney+ on Tuesday, Matalas opened up below to THR about how the show became another meditation on grief in the MCU, why he decided to have Vision and Tommy reunite with Billy but not Wanda — and that ominous mid-credits scene with Ultron. As the former showrunner of Picard, Matalas also pays tribute to Patrick Stewart, who died Oct. 28 at the age of 86: “I’d like to remember him kind of where we left him [in Picard], which was at that poker table surrounded by his friends laughing.”

In addition to writing episodes one, two and eight, you also directed episodes seven and eight — which really crack Vision open emotionally and pay off his relationships with Tommy and Ultron. What was most important to you when you were figuring out how to land the plane, so to speak, on VisionQuest? Why was this the right ending in your mind?

I do think that all endings need to touch on the beginning in some way. So honoring WandaVision by going back to the sitcom format as sort of the last battle was always our north star from the beginning of the writers’ room. We had a few different versions of it, but it felt like the right way to end it rather than just doing a rock and sock ’em robot battle royale — which we do, so we give Marvel fans their popcorn. We thought it would be fun to play out the final struggle with these two within this father-son sitcom. [A reference to] Sanford and Son is one of the first images you see in the first episode [of UltraVision], so we knew we were heading into a kind of All in the Family, Sanford and Son dynamic between Ultron and Vision.

You mentioned that Jac did not want to be creatively involved in VisionQuest, but does she know that you paid homage to her with this show-within-a-show format?

No, as far as I know, she doesn’t have an idea.

There are so many fun little WandaVision Easter eggs in UltraVision, but I particularly loved flipping through all of the wacky episode titles. You came up with so many of them!

I actually did those in post. I think we had generated a list early on from a few different writers, but ultimately that came together in post. It’s the most fun ever. We kind of wish we saw every one of those episodes. I remember when we screened it for Kevin Feige, one of the questions I asked just to double check was, “Does UltraVision go on too long?” And he cut me off immediately and yelled, “No!” He’s like, “It could go on for another 90 minutes, and I would’ve watched every minute of it.” So it was a big swing. We were really scared. We didn’t know if that was going to work, and as of this moment, it hasn’t aired, so I don’t know if it has. (Laughs.) So we’ll see.

For all the theatrics of UltraVision, which turns out to be an ineffective way for Vision to appeal to Ultron’s better angels, Vision knows that the only way he can stop Ultron from using the nanobots as a weapon of mass destruction is by forcing him to feel the grief of losing Jocasta. What did you want those final one-on-one conversations between Vision and Ultron to represent?

I think Vision says it best, which is that we couldn’t process this alone, and that grief really is about opening up and bringing it to light, as is all pain and trauma. I hope that that’s the message people walk away with, which is you can’t really just bury it in your code. You really do have to face it head on, and it’s very hard to do it alone.

Why do you think Vision is the only one who is able to get through to Ultron in the end?

I think Vision is the only one he respects, whether that is because of Ultron’s own ego and that Vision was sort of his own vision, if you will, as to what he could be. But we always knew we wanted to take Ultron into a place from the comics. Ultron fell in love with Jocasta in the original comic books, and bringing him along into the same kind of journey that Vision had been facing all season felt like the right story for those two to truly understand each other by the end.

We had a few different versions [of Ultron’s final scene]. We had a deleted scene in which Jocasta actually was sitting with Ultron in the mansion at the end and had survived. And now, we just sort of hint that he’s going to, at some point, bring her back. And then the question is: Will that start the cycle all over again? Is he going to be doing the same thing Wanda did or Vision did, and not really face his grief and then find another way to bring back his loss? And would she even want that? So it felt like the right end of the circle, if you will.

You’re referring to the mid-credits scene of Ultron holding onto a hard drive labelled “Jocasta.” Why did you choose to include that final scene? Was that a directive from Marvel?

We were all so in love with Jocasta and [wanted] a promise that she would continue on in some way. Again, we had a deleted scene in which she magnificently survived. I think that scene will maybe one day see the light of day, but it sort of, in totality, robbed the finale of its punch a bit when we had it there. But there were no true directives from Marvel other than Tommy was going to meet Vision, and that by the end, cold white Vision would return to his original red self. That’s a pretty blank canvas to work from. Working with Marvel was truly wonderful and collaborative in every way.

Paul Bettany told me that Marvel’s initial plan was always to center VisionQuest around Vision and Tommy, but did you always plan to bring Billy back into the fold as well?

You had to. The end of Agatha was [Agatha and Billy saying], “Let’s go find Tommy.” I think it would’ve been terrible and not very satisfying to not see the boys reunited with their father by the end.

Did you ever consider introducing Billy earlier in the story, or were you always planning to bring him back to save Vision alongside Tommy in the finale?

We entertained it; we talked about it. But if Billy came back early, it robbed Tommy and Vision of their own story and alleviated too much tension too early, and wasn’t as emotional as when he comes back and saves the day in the last moment when they need him most. I didn’t want to do that to Billy. I didn’t want to make him a supporting character in someone else’s struggle, so really earning Billy felt like the right way, to us, to do it.

What were those days like on set for you to watch Paul, Ruaridh and Joe together on screen for the first time? Were both of Billy’s scenes filmed on the same day?

We had the scene with Tommy and Billy where they first connect psychically — that was on another day [before the father-sons reunion]. Those boys were so much fun to direct. We were in this tiny room that was about a thousand degrees because we lit about 800 candles. They were just so down to play. There are a couple of deleted fun bits that we came up with on the spot that will come out, but they had a great chemistry and we would be excited to see more of those two together in the future as well. But as far as the end where Billy returns to save the family there, I think maybe we had two hours to do all that. It’s television and you don’t have the luxury of the time, but it was great. Joe’s wonderful and so down to try new things, as is Ruaridh. We were fortunate that the father and sons had great chemistry.

In their final scene together, Tommy asks Vision if he thinks there is any chance, with the two of them and Billy still around, that they may see Wanda again. In a callback to WandaVision, Vision tells Tommy, “We have said goodbye before, so it stands to reason… we’ll say hello again.” Was that line your idea, or did it come out of a collaboration with Paul or the rest of the writers?

It was my idea. As I was writing it, even though that Vision wouldn’t know that Hex Vision said that, so much of his soul was the same that it felt right that he would say the same thing he said to Wanda at the end of WandaVision. And we had to ask the question! For me, you couldn’t not address, “Are we going to see Mom again?” I would be sad if I watched a show, with all this magic and reunion out there, where they weren’t asking that question of, could it be possible [to see her again] in this universe?

You have certainly left the door open for a Maximoff family reunion in the near future. Did you ever have any discussions with Paul or the rest of the creative team about Wanda returning in the VisionQuest finale?

Yes, of course. It’s a thing that comes up constantly. Paul and I did experiment with a moment as he was dying, and it just felt like an added element in a big emotional sweep that was really about Vision and Ultron, and Vision, Tommy and Billy. It’s such a big idea to have Wanda there that you no longer pay attention to the rest of the arcs that are playing out. But I do feel like she’s very much in the room. My brilliant editor, Drew Nichols, found this shot of Wanda from WandaVision where she looks and smiles, and when he thinks of her and he’s talking about how love always leads to loss, I felt like we had her. I felt like we had honored her, but it didn’t really work to have her back in a dreamy way at the end.

Ruaridh Mollica has affectionately referred to Tommy and Billy as the “queer twin brothers” of the MCU, and he has openly talked about the personal significance of a bisexual actor being cast to play a bisexual character in such an expansive fictional universe. Given what is already established in the comics, did you ever consider alluding to Tommy’s bisexuality more explicitly in the show? Was there any reason that you chose not to this time around?

We do have a lot of Easter eggs to it. We wanted to start with Lisa [Molinari, played by Lauren Morais] because in the comics he had this relationship with Lisa coming right out of juvie, which we thought was interesting. But there wasn’t really a lot of time for him to be exploring his sexuality with the stakes so high. We definitely put in some queer and bisexual-coded patches; [for instance] there are these patches on his green jacket in the third episode. Those are promises, I suppose, for future stories and relationships. But with eight episodes, you got to pick one, and the stakes were very high for him to be flirting. (Laughs.)

Billy comes back to save the day wearing his signature blue crown, but Tommy’s green Adidas jacket is the closest we ever get to seeing him wear a super suit this season.

We had discussions about a super suit, and sort of like the moment with Wanda, if it’s not organic, it feels jammed in. We just could not find a logical reason for this kid to have a super suit. (Laughs.) There was no way that was not cheesy to do it. So we tried to get the closest thing we can to normal real world wear to honor his look so that maybe one day down the line we’ll have a super suit.

The last time we see Vision and Tommy on screen together in the finale, they are talking about having dinner with Billy in Eastview. How do you think Vision feels now that he has reconnected with and effectively has to parent both of his boys as young men?

I mean, that’s the thing I want to see, right? The family, at least for the most part, minus one critical component, is reunited. So what is that like now? You get a little dose of it with him telling Tommy saying, “I know if your mom was here, she’d want you to continue your education.” So I think Vision’s got to go be a dad, and I would love nothing more than to see what that’s like.

Have you had any conversations yet about working on future installments of the MCU? Is there a world in which VisionQuest could be expanded into an ongoing series, or did you always see this as a limited series?

I will say that we have so, so many ideas. And if I were having those conversations, there’s no way I could say that I was having those conversations. But who would not want to see this family again?

I was so sad to hear about the passing of Patrick Stewart, with whom you worked closely on Star Trek: Picard, and I’m very sorry for your loss. A lot of people on social media have thanked you for giving them the final gift of revisiting and saying goodbye to Patrick’s Picard, even though no one knew for sure that that would be the last time he’d play the character. Given that you began your career working on Star Trek: Enterprise, what did working on Picard with him mean to you personally, and how would you like to remember him?

I’d like to remember him kind of where we left him, which was at that poker table surrounded by his friends laughing. I was lucky enough to write and direct the last few moments of Captain Picard. It’s an honor I didn’t feel like I deserved, but feel blessed to have. The last scene with all of them, I really wanted to capture who he was around that cast. They were all dear friends and family in every way to him. What I did was I just let them actually play poker and joke and have fun. All of those smiles, all of those laughs from everyone and especially Patrick, were genuine. I wanted the fans in the world to see that because it’s an extraordinary thing to be around a cast like that, that truly loves each other that way.

I wanted to leave Captain Picard for everyone with all of them in a moment of joy and reunion, as opposed to him dying on the bridge of a starship or something like that. I like a happy ending — not always, but specifically in this case, this is how I wanted to leave that cast. It’s very kind for people to thank me, but I just played a small part in this universe and was honored to do it.

Do you remember the first time you met him? Was it when you were working as a PA on the Paramount lot and driving him around on golf carts?

Yeah, that’s exactly what it was. You do your research! (Laughs.) My first job in Hollywood was as a production assistant on Star Trek: Voyager, and I believe they started to shoot Star Trek: Insurrection within my first month. Merri Howard, who was my boss and mentor, pulled me from the television show to work on that movie for a day and just take care of Patrick and drive him around and get him coffee and orange juice. And going from that kid who would sneak on to the bridge of the Enterprise E, to bringing him back to the Enterprise D, is such a surreal, unbelievable journey. It’s a very Hollywood dream come true, and I just feel lucky to have been part of Star Trek for so long and hope to continue someday with more of it.

All episodes of VisionQuest are now streaming on Disney+.

#695. Frankie Muniz Hospitalized After Crashing Race Car at Daytona

“Malcolm in the Middle” star Frankie Muniz was rushed to a Florida hospital on Wednesday after he crashed during a practice lap at a Veterans Day event at the Daytona International Speedway.

Muniz, who picked up a second career as a racing driver in 2006, was scheduled to race as part of Team Air Force for Ford’s “Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic” event on Wednesday. But during a practice lap while the track was closed to the public, according to Entertainment Tonight, Muniz crashed his car. He was later taken to a local hospital and will no longer participate in the event, according to ET. Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings

Representatives for Muniz and Ford Racing did not respond to an immediate request for comment. A Ford Racing spokesperson told People that Muniz was “taken to a local medical facility for further evaluation and is awake and alert,” but they did not provide an update on his condition.

“Malcolm in the Middle” co-star Bryan Cranston, who joined Muniz in the show’s four-episode revival earlier this year on Disney+, was also set to appear at the event to support him, according to ET.

Muniz has maintained his racing career even as he made small returns to acting throughout the 2020s. He participated in NASCAR’s Craftsman Truck Series for the last three consecutive seasons, filming the “Malcolm in the MIddle” revival last year around his racing schedule. He finished 25th in this year’s Craftsman series.

“I was the first person that they ever had to work around cause normally like an actor is committed to the acting,” Muniz told Fox Sports’ Bob Pockrass last year. “But obviously I was a race car driver before they greenlit this show.”

#694. Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive

Mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears. New evidence from mysterious gas emissions near an enormous Martian volcano suggests that heat and volcanic processes could still be present deep beneath the planet's surface.

Researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region. The findings suggest that gases from the planet's interior may be escaping through cracks in the surface, potentially revealing volcanic activity that has remained hidden until now.

An international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground. If confirmed, this would indicate that Mars still has dormant volcanic systems capable of releasing gases to the surface.

The European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in findings reported in 2021. On Earth, hydrogen chloride is frequently released through openings connected to magma, raising the possibility that similar processes could be occurring on Mars.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," says Daniel Mège, Professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the study published in Science Advances.

Mysterious Gas Emissions Defy Mars' Seasonal Pattern

The researchers noticed something unusual during early summer in the Martian northern hemisphere. Hydrogen chloride concentrations were unexpectedly elevated in a particular region, even though the gas normally becomes scarce at that time of year.

Hydrogen chloride levels on Mars generally follow a seasonal cycle. They typically peak during northern winter before declining to very low levels in summer. Scientists believe much of this behavior is associated with the planet's dust and water cycles.

However, the observations revealed a striking exception. Elevated hydrogen chloride repeatedly appeared in early summer over volcanic fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons. The unusual timing and consistent location suggested that something beyond ordinary atmospheric chemistry might be responsible.

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, but scientists still do not know whether volcanic processes remain active beneath their surfaces.

Images taken from orbit indicate that some Martian volcanoes experienced eruptions within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes, demonstrating that the planet continues to experience seismic activity.

Together, these observations suggest that Mars may retain some of its geological energy. However, scientists have never directly observed a new volcanic eruption or fresh lava flow on the planet, leaving the question of present-day volcanism unresolved.

Fresh Cracks Reveal Clues to Hidden Volcanic Heat

To investigate the unusual gas concentrations, the research team combined atmospheric measurements with detailed observations of the Martian surface.

The Atmospheric Chemistry Suite aboard TGO uses infrared spectrometers to identify gases in the atmosphere. These instruments detected hydrogen chloride concentrated in a relatively small area shortly after the disappearance of winter frost.

Researchers then examined the same region using the orbiter's CaSSIS camera. The images revealed narrow fractures that appeared relatively fresh, with some extending hundreds of meters across the surface. Unusual changes in surface color were also visible around the cracks.

"The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," explains Daniel.

One possible explanation is that gases originating from magma deep underground travel upward through these fractures. On Earth, comparable volcanic openings are known as fumaroles.

The researchers propose that extremely cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to -120°C, allow ice to seal the fractures and temporarily prevent gases from escaping. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice sublimates, changing directly into vapor and potentially opening pathways for underground gases to reach the atmosphere.

The discoloration observed around the fractures could also be significant. It may result from minerals or other substances deposited by escaping gases, similar to the deposits commonly found around fumaroles (volcanic gas vents) on Earth.

Although the connection between the gas emissions and volcanic fractures appeared promising, the researchers needed to rule out other explanations.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," concedes Daniel.

The team carefully evaluated the chemical reactions that could produce hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere, including processes unrelated to volcanism.

"A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food," adds Daniel.

After examining the atmospheric and geological evidence together, the researchers proposed that the gas could be escaping from a dormant magma chamber beneath Alba Mons. Such a chamber would form part of an underground volcanic system that could continue releasing gases even without producing visible eruptions.

Hidden Volcanic Activity Could Help Mars Support Life

The implications may extend beyond understanding the planet's geological history. Volcanic gases could also provide clues about how Mars evolved and whether it ever supported environments suitable for life.

In the distant past, gases released from magma, including hydrogen chloride, may have helped create a denser atmosphere and warmer conditions. Those conditions could have allowed liquid water to remain across large portions of the Martian surface.

Volcanic activity might also create habitable environments underground. If rising magma or lava comes into contact with groundwater, the interaction can produce warm hydrothermal systems. Such environments could provide both chemical energy and protection from the harsh conditions on the surface.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," ponders Daniel.

Although the findings do not establish that Mars is currently erupting or that life exists beneath its surface, they offer an intriguing new reason to investigate the volcanic fractures around Alba Mons.

"These findings may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet," highlights Colin Wilson, ESA's project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

#693. Adam Conover May Be Getting Vulnerable on Stage, But He’s Still Riled Up About a Hollywood in Decline

The comedian and writer's latest stand-up special, 'Big Divorce Energy,' talks about an unexpected dip into personal material and the merger impact he says we're only starting: "We tried to avert the asteroid coming and we failed."

There are two Adam Conovers. One, the guy you probably know the best, played a satirical know-it-all on Adam Ruins Everything and has gone on to become a champion of the Hollywood working class. Other Adam, the guy he says a lot of people don’t know as well, is a touring stand-up whose recent demise of a 15-year-relationship has inspired him to delve to some real personal material.

The latter lays everything pretty bare in Big Divorce Energy, his recent hour that dropped Oct. 23 on his YouTube channel. It’s a pivot for anyone who just knows him from his TV work or his penchant for opining on podcasts. “I had always directed my comedy outwards,” says Conover, “talking about the world and things in the world, issues, history, politics, science, informing people of things. I had never really turned inward.” Related Stories TV Lana Condor, Anthony De La Torre Team for Rom-Com Microseries for Fetch (Exclusive) Business Piers Morgan Wants to Conquer America's Midterm Election Coverage

Looking inward involved candor about dating and sex in the wake of his split from illustrator Lisa Hanawalt, who worked on BoJack Horseman and created the Netflix series Tuca & Bertie. They remain friends and Hanawalt even gave her ex a particularly good note as he was refining the set, helping him move some things around to find the right joke to land on: a delightfully crude punchline that may offend the always even-keeled DC fandom.

“I’m on this quest to understand myself and my sexuality, especially what drives straight men, men who grew up straight or identify as straight in America,” he says. “Because I think that our sexuality is kind of the great unexamined frontier… I think straight men are the most sexually repressed people.”

In any conversation with Conover — and you can listen to the full thing on Spotify, Amazon Music or Apple — one can’t help but dig into his thoughts on the industry. During the 2023 strikes, he became one of the most biggest advocates for Hollywood unions and outspoken members of the WGA. He has railed against merger culture and, even a month after it was formalized, a post calling Skydance’s once looming acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery a “disaster” is still pinned atop his Instagram page. Now that it’s all done and dusted, he has not changed his tune. “We tried to avert the asteroid coming and we failed,” he says. “Now it’s coming and we’re all gonna face the consequences.”

His frequently strong words for the people who essentially write his checks beg the question: has he seen a negative impact on his work? Conover doesn’t see it that way, and he’s the first to say that everyone but those at the very top agree with him. “There’s a long tradition of my type of comedian being antagonistic towards the network brass,” he says. “On Adam Ruins Everything, we talked about the cable monopolies and advertising and stuff like that. That’s why the audience likes me. And so if they want to work with me, to get my audience, then that’s what they’re gonna get.”

But Conover also knows that those companies aren’t buying his particular brand of comedy at the moment, which is why he elected to self-release the new hour instead of shopping it around.

“The companies have given up on what I do and sort of pushed me to new media,” says Conover. “David Zaslav could [have given] a living wage and health insurance for people to write a bunch of comedy that he gets to own and monetize, but he and David Ellison and Ted Sarandos don’t want to do that anymore. Instead, I’ve got to build my own business on YouTube.”

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program and set the stage for the Apollo progam to land on the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin. NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program. Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11, and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13.

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview. "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station. As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon.

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

Jessica Chastain is returning to Broadway in “Lost Lear,” a play that puts a meta spin on “King Lear.”

Chastain was last on Broadway in “A Doll’s House,” an acclaimed 2023 revival of the Henrik Ibsen drama; this is her first time appearing in a new show.

In “Lost Lear,” she will portray Joy, a middle-aged actress suffering from early onset dementia, whose one clear memory is performing in the Shakespeare classic. Chastain will star alongside Corey Stoll (“Appropriate”) and Michael Urie (“Once Upon a Mattress,” “Spamalot”), with additional casting to be announced at a later date. Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings

Dan Colley wrote the show and will direct in his Broadway debut. Here’s the official logline: “As her grip on the present slips, Joy (Chastain), a former actress, is certain she’s back in rehearsal for ‘King Lear.’ At her care home, her nurse (Urie) takes his cues from her, stepping into whatever role she needs him to play. When her estranged son Conor (Stoll) comes to visit, he’s ready to tell his mother what he’s spent years leaving unsaid. But if he wants her to hear him, he’ll have to step into the scene. A limited event. A memory that will be impossible to leave behind.”

“Lost Lear” will premiere next spring at the Booth Theatre, with previews beginning on March 29, 2027 ahead of opening night on April 23. It will run for a limited 16-week engagement. The play was first workshopped and performed in Ireland in 2022 and has since been staged in various parts of the world, including New Zealand, the U.S., the U.K., Poland and Scotland.

“I never imagined, when we first made ‘Lost Lear,’ that it would one day be on Broadway — and I’ve imagined some pretty wild things,” Colley said. “I’m so thrilled to have the opportunity to share this piece with New York audiences and to discover new facets of the work through collaborating with this remarkable company of artists.”

#690. Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago

A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects. By examining ancient cannabis seeds and chemical traces preserved in human hair, researchers have uncovered new clues about the role of the plant in prehistoric burial rituals.

Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge. Flowers, leaves, and resins tend to decompose over time, leaving little physical evidence behind. Ancient communities also relied on cannabis for practical purposes, including producing fiber and oil, making it difficult to distinguish these uses from medicinal or recreational consumption.

An international team led by Dr. Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia. The burial site belonged to prominent members of the Scythians, a culture known for its skilled horseback riders who inhabited the vast Eurasian steppe.

Ancient Siberian Tomb Contains 1,000 Cannabis Seeds

During the investigation, researchers recovered approximately 1,000 cannabis seeds from the tomb. They used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of six individual seeds. Combined with other dating evidence, the results indicate that the seeds were deposited in the burial site during the early eighth century B.C.

"The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial," says Caspari, an archaeologist and the study's lead author.

The researchers also analyzed human hair preserved in the tomb's central burial chamber. Chemical evidence in several samples pointed to cannabis consumption, providing a crucial connection between the plant remains and the people buried at the site.

"This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body," says Caspari.

The findings were published in the journal Science.

Chemical Traces in Ancient Hair Reveal Cannabis Use

Although the cannabis seeds were remarkably well preserved, their presence alone could not establish whether the plant was used for its mind-altering effects. The seeds probably came from wild cannabis plants, and researchers could not determine whether people had deliberately cultivated them for their psychoactive properties.

The strongest evidence came from the preserved human hair. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, the team identified clear chemical signals consistent with cannabinol (CBN) in several samples.

CBN can form when tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound responsible for cannabis intoxication, undergoes oxidation. The researchers also detected weaker signals that matched the mass of THC, further supporting the possibility that the individuals had consumed cannabis.

While these chemical findings indicate cannabis use, they cannot reveal how much was consumed or exactly how the compounds entered the body. The individuals may have inhaled cannabis smoke or consumed the plant in another way, but the available evidence cannot establish a particular method.

Other archaeological discoveries from later periods in Central Asia provide clearer evidence of cannabis inhalation. At those sites, researchers have identified cannabinoid residues on heated stones and inside vessels, pointing to the use of heat to release compounds that could be inhaled.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," says Caspari, who conducts research at the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute for Geoanthropology in Jena (Germany).

Cannabis, Horse Sacrifices, and Ancient Burial Rituals

The cannabis evidence was discovered within an elaborate ceremonial burial site, suggesting that the plant may have been connected to important Scythian funerary traditions.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," says Gino Caspari.

Earlier research at the site identified the remains of 18 horses that had been deliberately positioned on the burial mound. Continued excavations have since uncovered evidence of several dozen more sacrificed horses, along with scattered human bones.

These discoveries reveal the extraordinary scale of the burial ceremonies and provide important context for understanding why cannabis may have been included among the materials deposited in the tomb.

Oldest Directly Dated Evidence of Cannabis Intoxication

Taken together, the seeds and chemical traces in human hair represent the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence currently known for cannabis use associated with intoxication.

However, several questions remain unanswered. The researchers cannot determine how much THC the ancient cannabis contained, whether the plants were particularly potent, or whether Scythian communities had begun deliberately selecting or cultivating cannabis varieties with higher concentrations of psychoactive compounds.

To investigate these questions, the team is now studying genetic material recovered from the ancient plant remains. The unusually good preservation of the cannabis DNA could provide valuable insights into how humans domesticated the plant and how it spread across different regions over thousands of years.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," says Gino Caspari. "DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon."

#689. A Rom-Com Connoisseur Goes Into Business With the True Story of a Sex Toy Saleswoman

Andy Tennant and Jessica Alba take on the task of empowering the sex-curious women of the Bible Belt in the AFM-bound 'The Fun Lady.'

Andy Tennant has always been led by the strong women in his life.

The American filmmaker and screenwriter is certainly an expert in the rom-com department, having helmed 2002’s Sweet Home Alabama with Reese Witherspoon and the Will Smith-led Hitch in 2005, two undeniable titans of the genre.

But for Tennant, who also directed 2008’s Fool’s Gold and 2010’s The Bounty Hunter, his latest project has never encompassed that connection to female resilience so well. “I’ve always felt in literature and everything else that female characters are so much more interesting than male characters, especially in movies,” he begins to The Hollywood Reporter. “Because male characters and [male] movie stars, their character doesn’t learn anything. Women’s stories… They’re so much more. They’re allowed to be eager, to be more vulnerable, to be more curious. And those stories I’m naturally drawn to.” Related Stories Movies China's Film Industry Arrives at AFM on a Domestic High Movies Can Constantin Survive Its Own Parent Company?

It’s befitting, then, that The Fun Lady — produced by Highland Film Group and headed to AFM — is not only getting the Andy Tennant treatment, but honoring one of the wildest true stories in the sex-toy industry. Linda Brewer, then 59, was the subject of a New York Times Magazine story in 2004 titled “Everything a Happily Married Bible Belt Woman Always Wanted to Know About Sex but Was Afraid to Ask.” It chronicles her rise from Arkansas high school dropout to becoming one of the top sellers for Passion Parties, a California-based company whose products included edible lotions, sex manuals, erotic games, lingerie and, crucially, an array of vibrators. Sure, she made sales of up to $140,000 in a single year, but Brewer also did the unthinkable: Smashed taboos and empowered the sex-curious, unsatisfied women of the Bible Belt.

In The Fun Lady, Brewer is depicted by superstar Jessica Alba (also producing the feature under her Metalmark Entertainment banner). She plays golden girl Mora, who retreats to her parents’ small Arkansas hometown when her picture-perfect life falls apart. Here, jobs are scarce, and gossip is a way of life. Desperate for a fresh start, she begins selling sex toys. The only problem is her absolute ignorance about pleasure, having never experienced an orgasm. Against all odds, Mora becomes “The Fun Lady,” crashing living rooms, shocking church ladies, and turning awkward sales parties into the hottest invitation in town. Along the way, she ignites a sexual revolution among women who have spent their lives pretending everything is fine.

Tennant, upon reading Mark Steilen’s (Tag, Shameless) script, was instantly hooked. “I thought, ‘You got to be kidding me!'” he recalls, chuckling to THR. “It’s such a lovely movie.” It’s not a romantic comedy, but he believed it to be very Sweet Home Alabama-adjacent. “The fact that it was based on a true story… I just found it incredible, and what a great jumping-off point for a story about not only human sexuality but relationships and the suppression of female sexual identity.” Importantly, for Tennant, it isn’t “comedy with a capital C.” The Fun Lady grapples with the human condition and the relationships that inform it, which, for him, “is what I’ve tried to do in pretty much every movie I’ve done.”

With production set to kick off early next year, Tennant is relieved to have a professional like Alba on board. “Casting has basically made my job a whole lot easier,” he says, reflecting on the myriad of A-listers that have stood in front of his camera. “[The Fun Lady] doesn’t need to cost any more than it’s going to cost. But we needed somebody who really got the material and understood that it wasn’t going to be a comedy with a bunch of cheap laughs. And Jessica, in my first conversation with her, [I could tell] she’s incredibly smart.”

Alba is not unlike the real-life person her role is inspired by: tenacious and a natural businesswoman. “She’s an entrepreneur,” Tennant continues. “She’s made an enormous success out of her business [consumer goods brand The Honest Company], and her conversations with me were [I was] like, ‘Oh, wow, I really need to be on my toes here.’ Because she takes it incredibly seriously. It is a comedy but there’s an awful lot of thematic issues that she really wants to bring to the fore,” he says, for example, women’s sexuality and marriages that play out “in a selfish way.”

Tennant is more than happy to let Alba — and a slew of cast members THR is not yet privy to the identities of — take the lead. “This is not false humility, but most of the time I try and stay out of the way,” he explains. “I set the camera and create an environment where everybody feels safe and willing to try things, and lot of what I love about prep actually is the conversations that happen with all the individual characters about what they’re thinking, what they’re afraid of, what they’re not sure of, and it challenges me.” Rather poetically, he actually likens the experience to heading up an orchestra: “We’ve got the bassoon and we’ve got the double bass and we’ve got the French horn and the violin. What we’re trying to create is a group that when they’re all together, has a wonderful harmony.”

What would have been a real weapon at their disposal during the shoot is the input of Brewer, who Tennant confirms has passed away. Although, he says, she was involved “quite a lot” with Steilen during the writing process. “Mark pursued the story. He spoke to her many, many times. And I know that her children are still very much wanting to see this movie made,” says the filmmaker.

And with Alba, he’s attempted to honor Brewer’s legacy by fleshing out the women of this story as much as possible. “We’ve tried to expand on the many women and the passion parties — no two are alike,” Tennant maintains. “The relationships are different. Their issues are different, and so we wanted to explore a lot of that. Somebody might not relate to Jessica’s character as much as they might relate to somebody else, and go, ‘Oh, I was there once in that relationship,’ or ‘I’m still in it.’ It doesn’t matter if it’s 1988 or 2000 or 2027. Sometimes, it’s hard to say what you want, say what you need, and it definitely affects your relationship.”

And if he’s honest with himself? Tennant didn’t have very many edits at all. “I actually said to Mark, ‘This is one of the few scripts that I’ve ever been offered that I haven’t had to do a ton of triage or work or rewrite or bring in other writers.’ In this case,” he adds, “the material was really, really strong.”

And when Tennant, the man behind the onscreen love affairs of Matthew Perry and Salma Hayek (in Fools Rush In) or Drew Barrymore and Dougray Scott (Ever After), casts his mind back to some of his favorite comedies of all time, such as Tootsie or the work of Sydney Pollack and Mike Nichols, what gives them their standout status is that unsuspecting warmth — and vital messaging — underneath those layers of fun and frill. “If I can just aspire to that level of intimacy and honesty and humor and real, honest character work…” says Tennant, trailing off. “If you laugh, you laugh. But maybe you’ll leave the theater thinking a little bit more about your relationship.”

#688. Tarantino Fired Mélanie Laurent From ‘Inglourious Basterds’ After ‘Terrible’ Table Read and Axed Isabelle Huppert for Not Showing Up: ‘I Don’t Owe You Jack S—‘

Quentin Tarantino gets brutally honest in Jay Glennie’s new book, “The Making of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds,” about his decision to fire Mélanie Laurent and Isabelle Huppert before production started on his 2009 revisionist World War II movie. Laurent ended up being rehired for the leading role of Shosanna Dreyfus, a French cinema owner seeking revenge against the Nazi officer who killed her family.

“Mélanie Laurent’s table read was terrible. It wasn’t good enough to be terrible,” Tarantino told the author (via People). “The most exciting day of preproduction is for me the table read. That is the closest I get to seeing the movie for the first time. Up until then, it’s just been me reading all the scenes to myself or to a friend … so a table read with the whole cast is so exciting and so important to me. Well, Mélanie was terrible, so I fired her.” Related Stories 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs

Laurent called Tarantino days after the table read to get her job back. She told the director she was not feeling well at the time and that she planned to fly herself back to Germany and put herself up at a hotel in order to read for him again. Tarantino admired Laurent’s passion and agreed to “turn the clock back” and “return to square one” with her as long as she was willing to go through three days of rehearsal with him. Whatever Laurent did doing those fateful few days impressed Tarantino enough for him to give the role of Shosanna back to her.

“Let me just go on the record for everybody to know: I love Mélanie,” Tarantino said. “The fact of the matter is, if we were not talking about the making of ‘Inglourious Basterds,’ I would never think about the table read again for the simple reason Mélanie is my Shosanna. She did a wonderful job. But we have decided to dive deep into the making of the movie with this book, and this is an important part of its history. You know, we agreed, warts and all. So, if we had not agreed to talk about the shooting of the movie, it would be out of my mind, and I would never think about it again.”

Isabelle Huppert, however, was not so lucky. She was fired by Tarantino and her role of Madame Ada Mimieux, a woman who shelters Shosanna in Paris, was given to the iconic “In the Mood for Love” star Maggie Cheung. Huppert “didn’t show up” to the table read, Tarantino said. “So fuck it. I fired her. I mean, I love Isabelle Huppert — ‘Heaven’s Gate’ and all that — but there were issues with her contract. It just kept stalling. And then not coming to the table read. Well, we cast Maggie instead.”

“That invariably happens,” the director continued. “As far as I’m concerned, if you’re cast and you are not at that table, I don’t owe you jack shit! You can be fired, especially if I get excited by what somebody else did in your absence.”

Unfortunately, all of the scenes that included Madame Ada Mimieux were cut out of the movie because Tarantino felt they over-explained things too much to the audience. As the director said: “Maggie was fantastic in the movie, but you just didn’t need to know how Shosanna acquired the cinema. All we needed was a title card saying ‘Four Years Later’ and Shosanna explaining that she inherited it from her aunt.”

“Inglourious Basterds” world premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May 2009, where it won best actor honors for Christoph Waltz, and then opened in theaters that August, where it became a box office hit with $321 million worldwide. The film remains one of Laurent’s signature roles.

“I have no moral compass when it comes to giving roles to actors: They have to be right. They have to feel like they are right for the world I have created,” Tarantino said about his freewheeling approach to hiring and firing actors. “I have fired actors in the past. If it’s not right, it is not right. I don’t owe them shit. I owe my film the best actors I can find. Period.”

“The Making of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds” is now available for purchase.

#687. A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, new research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

A new study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

"We expected aim to matter," said Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much."

The effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how quickly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A New Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

Earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

The new system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

"Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore said. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it."

Moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid."

A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

"You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he said. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid."

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches."

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast

The new computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

The software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

These calculations are important because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

"Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth

Despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research shows that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

"Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully," Moore said. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day."

The new simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

For one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

Nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.
